Description_Simple:
Title: Top Three Maximum Integers Finder

Main goal: This program reads up to 10 non-negative integers (each < 10000) from standard input, ignores invalid lines, and then identifies and prints the three largest values in descending order, each on its own line.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads up to 10 non‐negative integers (each between 0 and 10 000) from standard input (ignoring blank lines, non‐numeric input, and values outside the range). Once input is exhausted or 10 valid numbers have been read, it scans the collected numbers exactly once to track the largest, second‐largest, and third‐largest values. Finally it prints those three values in descending order (largest first, then second, then third), one per line. If fewer than three valid numbers were supplied, the missing positions remain at their initialized value of 0.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Sum‐Based Message Dispatcher

Main goal: This program reads pairs of integers from standard input, computes their sum, and then—based on which numeric range the sum falls into—prints one of several hidden messages. All the output strings are stored in encrypted or XOR‐obfuscated form and are decrypted at runtime using MD5‐derived DES/Blowfish keys and simple XOR routines. The result is a highly obfuscated dispatcher that maps input‐sum ranges to specific textual responses.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program repeatedly reads two integers x and y from standard input, computes their sum s = x + y, and then classifies s into one of seven ranges. For each range it has a corresponding human-readable message (loaded as encrypted string literals and decrypted at class‐load time). Depending on which interval s falls into, it prints exactly one of those seven messages. All of the surrounding jumps, fake variables, encrypted Base64/DES/Blowfish literals, and dummy branches are purely obfuscation and do not affect the simple “read two ints, sum them, pick one message by comparing the sum against fixed thresholds, and print it” core logic.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Right-Triangle Classifier

Main goal: This program reads an integer N from standard input, then processes N lines each containing three integer side‐lengths. For each triple it:
1. Checks that all sides are within the valid range [2,1000]; if not, outputs “invalid.”
2. Otherwise identifies the largest side as the hypotenuse candidate and tests the Pythagorean condition (largest² == sum of squares of the other two). If it holds, outputs “right,” otherwise outputs “wrong.”

Internally, all literal strings (“invalid”, “right”, “wrong”, and the tokenizer) are stored in an encrypted form and decrypted at runtime.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads from standard input line by line. The very first meaningful line gives a single integer N (after splitting the line on a fixed delimiter), which is the number of triangle‐classifications to produce. Each subsequent nonempty line is split into tokens, and if it has exactly three integer tokens a, b, c:

1. It first checks whether all three values lie between 2 and 5 inclusive.  
   - If not, it appends an “invalid” label to the results list.  
2. Otherwise it identifies the largest of the three sides (call it L) and the other two sides (call them X and Y).  
   - It then compares L² to X² + Y²:
     • If L² > X² + Y², it appends the label “obtuse.”  
     • Otherwise it appends “acute.”  

It repeats this process until it has collected N labels (skipping lines that don’t have exactly three tokens). Finally it prints out each of the N labels on its own line.

Description_Simple:
Title: GCD and LCM Calculator
Main goal: Reads pairs of integers and for each pair computes and prints their greatest common divisor (GCD) followed by their least common multiple (LCM).
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program repeatedly reads pairs of non‐negative integers (longs) from standard input until EOF. For each pair (a, b), it computes and prints two values: first the greatest common divisor (GCD) of a and b, then their least common multiple (LCM). Internally it handles the cases a > b, a < b, and a == b, but the net effect is always to output “gcd lcm” for each input pair.

Description_Simple: This code is an obfuscated Java program that reads input lines one by one, reverses the characters of each line by swapping pairs up to the middle, and then prints out the reversed line. Supporting methods provide integer and object comparisons, and a Base64‐based string decoder is used only to initialize an empty string for newline output.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads lines from standard input until EOF and, for each line, reverses its characters and prints the reversed line (followed by a newline). All the convoluted branches, fake variables, encrypted literals, and conditional jumps serve only to hide this simple “read‐reverse‐print” loop.

Description_Simple:
Title: Price Growth Simulator

Main Goal: 
This code reads an integer N from the input, then starting from an initial value of 100 000, it applies N rounds of a 5% increase. After each increase it rounds the result up to the nearest 1 000. Finally, it prints the resulting amount as an integer.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads a single integer N from standard input and then simulates N growth‐steps on an initial value of 100 000.0. On each step it:

1. Increases the current value by 5% (i.e. value ← value + 0.05×value).
2. Rounds that result up to the next multiple of 1 000 (using Math.ceil(.../1000.0)×1000).

After performing N of these steps, it prints the final amount as an integer.

In short, it computes the balance of a 100 000 starting principal grown by 5% N times, rounding up to the nearest thousand after each growth.

Description_Simple:
Title: Applying Pairwise Swaps to an Integer Sequence and Printing the Inverse Permutation  
Main Goal: Read two integers n and m, then m comma-separated swap instructions. Start with the identity array [1…n], apply each swap (transposition) in order to that array, and finally for each value 1…n print the position at which it ends up (i.e. the inverse of the resulting permutation). The rest of the code is just obfuscated helpers for string decryption and basic utilities.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This Java program reads two integers N and M from standard input, then reads M pairs of integers (l, r). It builds an array A of length N with A[i] = i+1. For each of the M pairs, it walks through all indices i and does:

  • if l > A[i], set A[i] = r  
  • else if r > A[i], set A[i] = l  

After processing every pair, it collects all values that appear in A and prints them (in ascending order because it scans possible values 1…N and prints the matching indices +1). In other words, it starts each position at its own index, repeatedly “jumps” it to the opposite end of each input pair whenever that end is strictly larger than its current value, and finally outputs the set of endpoints reached.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Insertion Sort with Stepwise Output

Main goal: This program reads an integer N (1 ≤ N < 100), then reads N values (each 0 ≤ value < 1000), sorts them using insertion sort, and prints the entire array before each insertion pass (including the initial state) and once more at the end.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads an integer n from standard input, then reads n more integers into an array. It performs a straightforward insertion-sort on that array, and after each insertion step it prints the current contents of the array (space-separated on one line). When sorting is complete, it prints the final sorted array. All of the confusing gotos, fake branches and encrypted strings are purely obfuscation—underneath it’s just reading n values and running insertion sort with step-by-step output.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) Calculator

Main goal: This code reads two integers (separated by a space) from standard input, computes their greatest common divisor by enumerating divisors of the smaller number and the remainder from the Euclidean step, and prints the largest common divisor.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>  
This program reads two space-separated integers from standard input, brute-forces all positive divisors of each number, collects those divisors common to both, and finally prints the largest common divisor. In other words, it computes and prints the greatest common divisor (GCD) of the two input integers by enumerating and comparing their divisor lists rather than using the Euclidean algorithm.

Description_Simple:
Title: Non-Ugly Number Counter

Main goal: Read a sequence of integers from standard input and count how many of them are not composed solely of the prime factors 2, 3, 5, and 7 (i.e. are not “ugly” numbers).

Summary: The code first builds the list of all “ugly” numbers ≤ 9999 by sieving out any number divisible by primes ≥ 11 (and composites co-prime with 2,3,5,7). It then reads each input integer, skips it if it is in the ugly‐number list, and otherwise increments a counter. Finally, it prints the count of non-ugly numbers.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program builds a list of prime numbers up to 10 000 by a two-phase trial-division sieve—first sieving out multiples of 2, 3, 5, and 7 in the range 10–99, then sieving all candidates up to 10 000 against the accumulated primes. After constructing the full prime list, it reads whitespace-separated integers from standard input, tests each one for membership in the prime list, and finally prints the count of how many of the inputs were prime.

Description_Simple:
Title: Maximum Difference Calculator

Main goal:
This code reads an integer N from standard input, then reads N more integers into an array, and finally computes and prints the maximum difference arr[j]−arr[i] over all pairs with j>i (i.e. the largest “profit” you could get by buying at one position and selling later). If all later values are smaller than earlier ones, it prints the least negative difference (the smallest “loss”).
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads an integer N from standard input, then reads N further integers into an array. It then scans the array once to find the largest difference arr[j] – arr[i] with j > i (i.e. the maximum “profit” if you buy at arr[i] and sell later at arr[j]). If no later element exceeds an earlier one, it will return the (possibly negative) difference between the last and first entries. Finally it prints that maximum difference and exits.

Description_Simple:
Title: Bubble Sort with Swap Counting and Custom Delimiter

Main Goal:
This program reads an integer N and then N integers from standard input, sorts them in ascending order using the bubble-sort algorithm while counting the total number of swaps performed, and finally prints the sorted list (using a decrypted delimiter) followed by the swap count.

Key Components:
1. FastScanner: A highly obfuscated fast input reader for tokens, integers, longs, etc.
2. llIlIlIIlIIl / IIllIlIIlIIl / lIllIlIIlIIl: Simple helper methods that check “<”, “!= 0” (boolean), and “>” respectively to drive loops and comparisons.
3. IIlllIIIlIIl (and related cryptographic setup):
   - Uses MD5 of a key string (“VnMaG”) to create a Blowfish key.
   - Decrypts a Base64-encoded cipher text (“II1Xn/OvUcs=”) to obtain the delimiter string (e.g. “, ”) stored in lIllIIIlIl[0].
4. Main Sorting Logic:
   a. Read N and the array of N integers.
   b. Perform bubble sort:
      – Repeatedly scan the array, swapping adjacent out‐of‐order elements.
      – Keep a running count of how many swaps occur.
      – Stop once a full pass makes no swaps.
   c. Print the sorted numbers separated by the decrypted delimiter.
   d. Print the total swap count on a new line.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads an integer n and then n integers from standard input, sorts them in ascending order using a basic bubble‐sort pass that counts each swap, and finally prints the sorted list (separating elements by a single space) followed by the total number of swaps performed. The obfuscation layers (renamed variables, fake branches, encrypted helper strings, etc.) do not alter this core logic.

Description_Simple:
Title: Selection Sort with Swap Counting

Main goal: The program reads an integer n and an array of n integers from standard input, sorts the array in ascending order using a straightforward selection-sort algorithm while counting how many swaps are performed, and then prints the sorted array followed by the total swap count.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The obfuscated program simply reads an integer n, then reads an array of n integers. It performs a straightforward selection‐sort on the array, counting each time it swaps a smaller element into the current position. After sorting, it prints the array (numbers separated by spaces) on one line, and on the next line prints the total number of swaps performed. All of the rest of the code (weird branches, fake locals, encrypted strings, and helper methods) is only there to obscure this basic read–sort–print logic.

Description_Simple:
Title: Reverse Polish Notation (Postfix) Calculator

Main goal: This program reads a single line from standard input containing a whitespace-separated or contiguous postfix (Reverse Polish) arithmetic expression, uses a simple integer stack to parse multi-digit numbers and apply the operators +, -, *, and / in the proper order, and then prints the computed integer result.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program is a simple integer Reverse-Polish (postfix) notation calculator. It reads one line of input, scans through each character, and:

1. Parses contiguous digit characters into base-10 integers.
2. Pushes each parsed integer onto a custom stack.
3. When it encounters an operator character (+, –, *, /), it pops the top two values from the stack, applies the operator (left operand is the earlier‐pushed value), and pushes the result back on.
4. Ignores any other characters (e.g. whitespace).
5. After processing the entire input line, it pops and prints the final result.

The obfuscation is purely syntactic—renamed variables, bogus branches, encrypted strings, etc.—but the core algorithm implements a standard stack-based postfix expression evaluator over 32-bit ints.

Description_Simple: Simulates a round-robin scheduler: it reads the number of processes and a time‐slice quantum, then reads each process’s name and required CPU time. It repeatedly cycles through the process queue, giving each process up to one quantum of time; when a process finishes, it prints the process’s name and its completion time.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The obfuscated program is simply a Round-Robin scheduler simulator. It reads two integers N (number of processes) and Q (the time slice), then N pairs of “process name” (a string) and “burst time” (an int). It maintains a circular queue of processes, each with its remaining time. Repeatedly it:

1. Dequeues the next process whose remaining time > 0.
2. If its remaining time ≤ Q, it advances the global clock by that remaining time, prints “<name> <finish-time>” and effectively removes the process (remaining time becomes zero).
3. Otherwise it advances the clock by Q, subtracts Q from that process’s remaining time, enqueues it back, and prints “<name> <current-time>”.

It continues until all processes have run to completion, then exits.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Integer‐Array Intersection Counter

Main Goal:
This heavily obfuscated Java snippet reads two integer sequences (first the length, then the list, twice), assumes each list is sorted, and counts how many values appear in both lists.  Under the hood it swaps so the larger array is the “search space” and then, for each element of the smaller array, locates it in the bigger array via a custom multi‐pivot search. The final count of common elements is printed.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads two integer sequences from standard input—first an array A of size N, then an array B of size M—and computes the total number of “cross‐pairs” where an element of A is strictly greater than an element of B.  Internally, it even swaps them if the first array is smaller, so it always iterates over the smaller array B in the outer loop.  To speed things up, it partitions the (larger) array A into four equal segments (quartiles) and, for each b in B, first determines which quartile of A b falls into (by comparing b against the 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4–points of A) and then only counts the remaining A-elements in that segment that exceed b.  Finally it prints the sum of these counts.

Description_Simple:
Title: Standard Deviation Calculator

Main goal: The code reads successive data-sets from standard input. Each data-set begins with an integer N (1 ≤ N ≤ 1000) specifying how many values follow on the next line. It then reads N space-separated integers, computes the population standard deviation of those N values, and stores the result. The sequence of data-sets ends when N=0. Finally, it prints each computed standard deviation on its own line formatted to two decimal places.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads an integer N from standard input (exiting immediately if N ≤ 0). It then processes N data sets. For each data set it reads a line of integers, computes their arithmetic mean, and then calculates the population standard deviation:

  σ = sqrt( (1/N) · Σ₁ⁿ (xᵢ − mean)² ).

Finally it prints each data set’s standard deviation on its own line formatted to two decimal places.

Description_Simple: This Java program reads a line from standard input, parses it as an integer N, and checks that 1 ≤ N ≤ 100 using two helper methods. If N is out of range or not a valid integer, it throws and logs an exception. Otherwise, it computes N³ via Math.pow and prints the result. The static initializer and bitwise expressions are simply an obfuscation to set the lower bound to 1 and the upper bound to 100.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads a line from standard input, parses it as an integer n, and enforces that 1 ≤ n ≤ 100. If the input is not a number or falls outside that range, it throws and prints an exception stack trace. Otherwise it computes n³ (n to the third power) and prints the result.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Integer Parser and Calculator

Main Goal: This program reads up to four space-separated integers from the first line of standard input, reconstructs them from their digit characters, and then computes and prints two values: the product of the first and third integers, and twice the sum of the first and third integers.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This obfuscated program simply reads ASCII digit characters from standard input, line by line, assembles each line’s digits into an integer, and stores those integers in an array. After it has read all lines (or at least three numbers), it takes the first and the third numbers (call them A and C) and prints two values:

  1. The product A × C  
  2. Two times their sum, i.e. 2 × (A + C)

All the grotesque branching, dummy variables, encrypted strings, and fake code paths only serve to hide these few straightforward steps:  
– parse each input line as a base-10 integer  
– let A = first integer, C = third integer  
– compute A*C and 2*(A+C)  
– output them separated by a space.

Description_Simple:
Title: Find the Largest Square-Free Number ≤ N

Main goal:  
This program first builds a sieve of smallest prime factors for all integers up to a fixed limit (1000). It then reads an input N and searches downward from N to 1, testing each candidate k by factoring it (using the precomputed smallest‐factor array) and checking whether any prime appears more than once. The first k encountered with no repeated prime factors (i.e., k is square-free) is printed and the program exits. If no such k > 1 is found, it prints 1.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads an integer n (up to about 1000), builds a sieve of “smallest prime factors” for all numbers up to 1000, and then scans downward from n to find and print the largest integer ≤ n whose prime factorization contains no repeated prime (i.e. is square-free).  Concretely:

1. It allocates an array SPF[ ] of length ≈1000, and for each integer p starting at 2, marks SPF[multiples of p] = p.  
2. It reads n from input.  
3. If n<4 it just prints n (since 1,2,3 are all square-free).  
4. Otherwise for each i = n, n–1, …, 2:
   – it uses the SPF[] array to factor i by repeatedly dividing out SPF[i], counting exponents of each prime in a map.  
   – if all exponents are 1 (i.e. no prime squared divides i), it prints i and exits.  
5. If it falls through the loop, it prints 1.  

In short, the core logic finds and outputs the largest square‐free number not exceeding the given n.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Integer Comparator

Main Goal: This code reads two integers from standard input, verifies they lie within a predefined range, compares them, and prints one of three messages (“less than”, “equal to”, or “greater than”) or an out-of-range error. The messages and numeric limits are stored in encrypted form and are decoded at class‐load time.

Key Functions:
- llIlllIlIIl(): Initializes an array of integer constants used for bounds and control flow.
- IlIlllIlIIl(): Decrypts and populates the output strings using three helper routines:
  • lllIllIlIIl(): Base64 + XOR decryption.
  • IIIlllIlIIl(): Blowfish decryption with an MD5‐derived key.
  • lIIlllIlIIl(): DES decryption with an MD5‐derived key.
- IIllllIlIIl, lIllllIlIIl, IlllllIlIIl, llllllIlIIl, IIIIIIllIIl: Simple comparison helpers (<=, <, >, ==, >=).
- main(): Reads inputs, checks bounds, selects the proper comparison result, and prints the corresponding decrypted message.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads two integers x and y from standard input, each of which must lie between –1000 and +1000 (inclusive). If either value falls outside that range, it prints an “out of range” error message. Otherwise it compares x and y and prints exactly one of three messages:
  • “x is less than y”  
  • “x is greater than y”  
  • “x is equal to y”  

All other code (fake variables, bogus branches, string‐decryption routines, etc.) merely obscures this straightforward logic.

Description_Simple:
Title: “ABC” Substring Counter

Main Goal:
This program reads an integer N and then a string of length N, and counts how many times the substring “ABC” appears (possibly overlapping) in that string. It finally prints the total count.

Key Parts:
- A tiny array of integer constants is initialized to {0,3,65,1,66,2,67} (after de-obfuscation these map to 0, 3, 'A', 1, 'B', 2, 'C').
- In main(), it reads N and the character array of the input string.
- It slides a window from i=0 to i≤N−3 and checks if characters at positions i,i+1,i+2 are 'A','B','C'.
- Each match increments a counter.
- The counter is printed at the end.
- The rest of the code is an obfuscated fast input/output utility (FastScanner and FastWriter).
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads an integer N and then a string S of length N. It scans S from left to right (up to index N–3) and counts how many times the three‐character pattern “101” appears (i.e. S[i]=='1', S[i+1]=='0', and S[i+2]=='1'). It then prints that count. All the other methods, fake branches, encrypted strings, and renamed variables serve only to obscure this simple substring‐counting logic.

Description_Simple:
Title: Three-Number Sorting and Printing

Main Goal:
This obfuscated Java program reads three integers from standard input, compares them in every possible ordering (including equalities), and prints them out arranged in non-decreasing order.

Explanation of Key Parts:
1. Static Initialization  
   - A single-element int array is created and set to zero via bitwise operations. It is only used to initialize three local ints to zero.

2. Input Parsing  
   - Reads three tokens with Scanner.next(), parses them into integers a, b, c.

3. Comparison Methods  
   - lIIIllIlIll(int n, int n2): returns true if n == n2  
   - IIIIllIlIll(int n, int n2): returns true if n < n2  
   - IlIIllIlIll(int n, int n2): returns true if n > n2  

4. Sorting Logic  
   - A long chain of if/else-if conditions tests every combination of a < b < c, a < c < b, b < a < c, etc., plus cases where any two (or all three) are equal.  
   - In each branch it prints the three numbers in ascending (or non-decreasing) order.

5. Obfuscation Noise  
   - Dead code like `"".length()` and bitwise expressions in the conditionals have no effect on the actual sorting logic; they are only there to confuse a reader or decompiler.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads three space‐separated integer inputs, determines their relative order, and then prints them out sorted in ascending order (smallest to largest), separated by spaces. All of the convoluted branches and helper methods (e.g. lIIIllIlIll for “==”, IIIIllIlIll for “<”, IlIIllIlIll for “>”) simply enumerate the six possible orderings of three distinct values and pick the correct one to output. Any extraneous string operations, dead‐code branches, and encrypted literals are purely obfuscation; the core logic is just a three‐value sort and print.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Java Program That Reads Five Integers and Prints Hidden Messages Based on Comparisons

Main Goal: The code reads five integers from standard input, evaluates a fixed set of “≤” and “≥” constraints among them, and prints a corresponding hidden message for each satisfied condition. If none of the checks pass, it prints a default fallback message.

Key Points:
1. Static Initialization  
   - Builds an index array (IlIllIIlll) holding the integers 0 through 7 via obfuscated bit-twiddling and calls two setup methods.  
   - Constructs a string array (lIIllIIlll) of length 6, filling it with encrypted Base64 literals, each decrypted by one of three routines.

2. Decryption Routines  
   - IIIIlllIlIll: Uses DES with an MD5-derived key to decrypt a Base64 input.  
   - IlIIlllIlIll: Uses Blowfish with an MD5-derived key for Base64 decryption.  
   - lIIIlllIlIll: Decodes Base64 then applies a reversible XOR loop against a password.

3. Comparison Helpers  
   - IllIlllIlIll(a,b) returns (a ≥ b).  
   - lIlIlllIlIll(a,b) returns (a ≤ b).  
   - IIIllllIlIll(x) returns (x == 0).  
   - lllIlllIlIll(x) returns (x ≤ 0).

4. main() Workflow  
   - Reads one line, splits into five integers: a, b, c, d, e.  
   - Initializes a counter to zero.  
   - Executes four hard-coded if-blocks, each combining multiple calls to ≤/≥ on different pairs (and sums/differences) of the inputs.  
   - For each block whose condition is true, it prints the matching decrypted string and increments the counter.  
   - After all checks, if the counter is still zero, it prints a final fallback string.

In short, this is an obfuscated conditional dispatcher: it hides its messages behind DES, Blowfish, or XOR ciphers and only reveals them when certain numeric relationships among the five inputs hold.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads five space- (or delimiter-) separated integers from standard input: W, H, X, Y, and R. These represent the width and height of a rectangle (with its lower‐left corner at the origin), the (X,Y) coordinates of a circle’s center, and the circle’s radius R. It then checks where the circle falls relative to that rectangle:

1. If the entire circle lies strictly inside the rectangle (i.e.  
   R ≤ X ≤ W–R  and  R ≤ Y ≤ H–R),  
   it prints the “inside” message.

2. Otherwise, it tests each of the four single‐edge contact conditions in turn:
   – If the circle touches or crosses only the left edge (X–R ≤ 0 but Y fully in range), it prints the “left‐border” message.  
   – If it touches only the bottom edge (Y–R ≤ 0 but X in range), it prints the “bottom‐border” message.  
   – If it touches only the right edge (X+R ≥ W but Y in range), it prints the “right‐border” message.  
   – If it touches only the top edge (Y+R ≥ H but X in range), it prints the “top‐border” message.

3. If none of those single‐edge tests fire (meaning the circle lies completely outside or overlaps multiple edges/corners), it prints the “outside” message.

In short, despite heavy obfuscation, the core logic is just a routine to determine and report whether a circle of radius R at (X,Y) is fully inside, exactly touching one side of, or wholly outside a W×H rectangle.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Line‐Reader and Case‐Printer

Main Goal: This program reads up to 10 000 lines of standard‐input into an array, stopping early if it encounters a hidden “start” marker. It then walks through the stored lines and prints each one as  
 Case 1: <line>  
 Case 2: <line>  
…  
until it finds a second hidden “end” marker.  

The two sentinel strings are stored in encrypted form and are decrypted at class‐load time using a small DES+MD5 routine.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads up to 2,500 lines of text from standard input into an array, stopping early if it encounters a special “end‐of‐input” keyword (stored encrypted in the program). After the input phase, it then walks through the collected lines again and, for each one, prints

  Case k: <that line>

in sequence (with k starting at 1), stopping if it encounters a second special “stop‐printing” keyword (also stored encrypted). All the surrounding gotos, fake branches, dead code and string‐encryption routines are purely obfuscation; the real logic is just “read lines until marker1, then print them numbered until marker2.”

Description_Simple:
Title: Pair Integer Sorter with Sentinel Termination

Main Goal: This program reads lines from standard input, each containing two integers separated by a space. For each pair (a, b), it prints them in non-decreasing order (smaller first). It stops processing (without printing) when one of these sentinel conditions is met:
  • The pair is “0 0”  
  • The first integer is negative and the second exceeds 10000  
  • More than 3000 pairs have been read  

All of the obfuscation (bit tricks, DES decryption, confusing method names) serves only to hide these simple behaviors.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads lines from standard input, each containing two space-separated integers (a and b). It stops processing as soon as it encounters the special termination case (both numbers zero, or other sentinel conditions). For every normal input pair before termination, it prints the two numbers in non-decreasing order (smallest first). Behind all the obfuscation, its sole function is “read integer pairs until a stop condition, then for each pair output the numbers sorted ascending.”

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Solution for Counting Ways to Sum to S Using K Parts

Main goal:
This heavily obfuscated Java program reads two integers K and S from standard input and then computes how many ways you can write the integer S as a sum of K non‐negative integers. In other words, it solves the classic “stars and bars” or integer‐composition counting problem (the number of K-tuples (x₁,…,x_K) of non‐negative integers with x₁+…+x_K=S). The result is printed to standard output.

Summary description:
- The entry point `main` reads K and S, calls `g(S, K)`, and prints the result.
- Internally, `g(total, parts)` and its helper `f(remaining, parts)` implement a dynamic-programming recurrence that builds up the count of compositions by summing over valid last‐part choices.
- All array accesses, constants and control structures have been hidden behind layers of bit‐twiddling, encrypted string lookups, reflection of string‐lengths and tiny helper methods returning boolean tests, but at its core it is just a DP on sums of length K.
- The DP uses a rolling buffer (`IlllllIIll` array) of size K to store intermediate counts, starting with DP[0]=1, and then aggregates contributions until it recovers the final count for sum S.
- The rest of the code is devoted to decrypting embedded string constants (via AES/DES/Blowfish ciphers, Base64, MD5/SHA digests) and initializing obfuscated integer constants for indexes and lengths.
- Despite the obfuscation, the heart of the algorithm is simply counting integer compositions (combinatorial partition) with dynamic programming.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads two integers K and S from standard input and computes

   ∑_{i=0..K–1} ∑_{j=0..K–1} [i + j ≤ S]

—i.e. the number of ordered pairs (i, j), with 0 ≤ i< K and 0 ≤ j< K, whose sum does not exceed S. It does this by, for each i from 0 to K−1, adding min(K, S−i+1) (the count of j’s satisfying j≤S−i) and then prints the total.

Description_Simple:

Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>

Then it prints A / B as a floating-point number using a predefined format (e.g. with fixed decimal precision) via printf. Any obfuscation is only wiring around these three core operations.

Description_Simple:

Description_Detailed:

  • area = π * R²  
  • circumference = 2 * π * R

Description_Simple:

Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>

    <integer1> <operator> <integer2>

where `<operator>` is one of “+”, “–”, “*” or “/” (and there is a special operator token that, if seen, causes immediate termination of input processing). Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Java Sequence Analyzer

Main goal:
This heavily obfuscated Java program reads an integer N and then a line of N space-separated integers from standard input. It scans the array to locate the last adjacent pair where the second element exceeds the first, then builds a second array of length N + 2 whose entries at index i (for i≥2) equal the sum of the element two positions earlier in the input and the corresponding entry two positions earlier in the new array. Finally, it prints:
 1. The element at the identified index of the last ascending adjacent pair  
 2. The element immediately following that in the array  
 3. The computed value at index N of the new “every-other” cumulative-sum array  

In addition to the main logic, the code contains numerous decryption routines (using DES, Blowfish, Base64, MD5, etc.) that are solely used to reconstruct obfuscated string constants at runtime. These routines are never exercised in the main algorithm beyond initializing hidden messages and separators.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads an integer n, then reads a line of n space‐separated integers into an array A[0…n–1]. It then

1. Scans all adjacent pairs A[i],A[i+1] (for i=0…n–2) and records
   • “lastDrop” = the greatest index j such that A[j] ≥ A[j+1],
   • “lastRise” = the greatest index k such that A[k] < A[k+1].

2. Builds a new array S of length n+1 by
   • S[0]=0,
   • for i from 2 up to and including n: S[i] = A[i–2] + S[i–2].
   This has the effect that S[n] = A[n–2]+A[n–4]+…+A[p], where p is 0 if n is even, or 1 if n is odd (i.e. you sum every other element back from index n–2).

Finally it prints
   lastDrop + " " + lastRise + " " + S[n]

That is, the zero‐based positions of the last non‐increasing and last strictly increasing adjacent transitions, and the alternating‐step sum of the input array ending at index n–2.

Description_Simple:

Key Functions:

Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>  
This program reads a sequence of integer pairs (r, c) from standard input, each representing the dimensions of a rectangle, stopping when it sees the pair (0, 0).  It ignores any out‐of‐range pairs (valid ranges 1–44).  After the terminating (0, 0), it prints for each previously read pair a block of text consisting of r rows of c asterisk characters (“*”), with a blank line separating successive blocks.

Description_Simple: The program reads pairs of integers (width, height) until both are zero. It enforces bounds (width≥3, 1≤height≤300), stops on invalid input, and otherwise draws for each pair a hollow rectangle of the given dimensions. Three printable symbols used for top/bottom edges, left/right edges, and the interior are stored in obfuscated form—two via a simple Base64 + XOR routine and one via Blowfish decryption—and are revealed at runtime to render the ASCII art.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The program reads a sequence of integer pairs (width, height) from standard input. Input terminates when it encounters the pair (0, 0) or any pair outside the allowed bounds (width ≥ 3, height ≥ 1, width/height ≤ 300). For each valid pair it stores the dimensions and, after reading ends, iterates over them in order. For each stored (w, h), it prints an ASCII rectangle of width w and height h using three characters (a “corner” symbol, an “edge” symbol, and a “fill” symbol). It prints the corners at each of the four corners, the edges along the top/bottom and left/right sides, and the fill character everywhere else inside the rectangle. Different rectangles are separated by blank lines.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated ASCII Block‐Pattern Generator

Main Goal:
This code reads pairs of integers (height H and width W) from standard input until it encounters “0 0,” and for each nonzero pair it prints an H×W ASCII art pattern that alternates two block designs in a checkerboard‐like fashion. The actual characters used in the pattern are stored in an encrypted string array and decrypted at runtime.

Key Components:
1. Initialization:
   • lllIllIlIll(): Fills an integer array IIlIIllll with small constants (0,1,2,…).
   • IllIllIlIll(): Builds the string array llIIIllll by decrypting Base64 blobs via three methods:
     – llIIllIlIll: MD5+DES decryption
     – IIlIllIlIll: MD5+Blowfish decryption
     – lIlIllIlIll: Base64 decode + simple XOR cipher

2. Main Loop (main()):
   • Repeatedly reads two ints H and W.
   • If both are zero, exits.
   • Otherwise, divides H and W into 2×2 “tile” blocks:
     – Uses nested loops over tile rows (H/2) and tile columns (W/2).

     – Handles the case when H or W is odd by printing the remaining last row or column in the correct pattern.
   • After each pattern, prints a newline (also decrypted).

3. Utility Methods:
   • llIlllIlIll, lIIlllIlIll, IIIlllIlIll, IlIlllIlIll: simple numeric comparisons (==, !=, >=, <=).

In essence, it’s an intentionally obfuscated program that generates a checkerboard‐style ASCII art of a user‐specified size, using encrypted constants to hide the actual characters.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads pairs of positive integers (H, W) until it encounters a pair of zeros, and for each H×W pair it prints an H-row, W-column checkerboard (alternating) pattern using two symbols.  Even‐indexed rows use one 2‐symbol alternation (“symbol A” then “symbol B”), odd‐indexed rows swap those two, producing the classic checkerboard look.  After printing each H×W board, it loops back for the next input pair; upon reading “0 0” it exits.

Description_Simple: This program scans an integer N and then iterates from 3 up to N (stopping at 10000). For each number, it checks if it’s divisible by 3 or if any decimal digit equals 3 (units, tens, hundreds, or thousands place) and prints those that match.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>

All of the convoluted branches, fake jumps, encrypted literals, split‐and‐recombine operations, and range tests ultimately collapse into the single simple check “i % 3 == 0.”

Description_Simple:
Title: Fast I/O Utility Wrapper for a Competitive Programming Solver

Main Goal:
This code provides a highly optimized, byte‐level FastScanner for reading input (tokens, ints, longs, doubles, arrays) and sets up a PrintWriter for output. Its purpose is to supply ultra-fast input/output routines and then invoke a (not shown) Solver class’s run() method to process the problem’s logic.

Summary Description:
The `Main` class’s `main` method creates an instance of `FastScanner` (reading from `System.in`) and a `PrintWriter` (writing to `System.out`). It then constructs and runs `Solver`, passing in these I/O objects and ensuring output is flushed and closed, with exception handling.

Nested inside `Main`, the `FastScanner` class reads raw bytes into a buffer and exposes methods:
- `hasNext()`, `next()`: check for and return the next token as a String
- `nextInt()`, `nextLong()`, `nextDouble()`: parse the next token into primitive types
- `nextIntArray(n)`, `nextLongArray(n)`: read an array of length n of ints or longs

All comparisons and constants are obfuscated via bitwise operations, but the core I/O logic mirrors a typical competitive‐programming fast reader.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This obfuscated Java program is simply a standard competitive‐programming template that sets up fast I/O and then delegates to a `Solver` class (not shown) to do the actual work. Stripping away all the bogus branches, dead code and string‐encryption machinery, here is what it really does:

1. In `main`, it constructs a `FastScanner` (reading from `System.in`) and a `PrintWriter` (writing to `System.out`), then calls `new Solver(scanner, writer).run()`, flushing and closing the writer afterward.

2. The nested `FastScanner` class implements buffered input:
   – It reads raw bytes from `System.in` into a byte array.
   – It skips non-printable characters to find the start of the next token.
   – It provides methods to parse tokens as `String`, `int`, `long`, `double`, or arrays of those types.
   – It handles signs, range checks (e.g. detecting overflow), and throws the usual `NoSuchElementException` or `NumberFormatException` if input is missing or malformed.

All the convoluted integer comparisons, empty string operations, fake branches, encrypted literals and meaningless variables simply mask this straightforward scanner logic. The real algorithmic work is performed in the unseen `Solver.run()` method, which reads input via `FastScanner` and writes output via `PrintWriter`.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated “Missing Cards” Finder

Main goal: This program reads N card descriptions (each given by a suit name and a rank), marks those cards as “present,” and then prints out every card in a standard 52-card deck (13 ranks × 4 suits) that was *not* listed in the input.  

Summary_description  
- The code begins by building a 4×13 “default” matrix of card ranks 1–13 for each of the four suits.  
- It then reads an integer N and N lines of (suitString, rank) pairs.  
- Based on the decrypted suit names (“Spade”, “Heart”, “Club”, “Diamond”), it sets entries in a second matrix to mark which cards appeared in the input.  
- Finally it walks through all 4×13 positions; whenever the default rank (j+1) does not match the entry in the “seen” matrix (i.e. the card was missing), it prints out the suit initial (S/H/C/D) and the rank.  
- To foil static analysis, suit‐name constants are stored encrypted and decrypted at runtime via DES and Blowfish routines, and the whole thing is packed with meaningless loops, bit-twiddling constants, and dummy string‐length checks.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program builds an R×C integer grid where each row i contains the numbers 1,2,…,C. It then reads R input lines (each line is a row‐name plus an integer k) and, for each line, marks the cell in that named row at column k. Finally it scans every cell of the grid and whenever the marked grid value differs from the original (i.e. the cell was never “hit” by an input line), it prints a one‐letter code for that row together with the expected number for that cell.

Concretely:
1. It decrypts four row labels (e.g. “S”, “H”, “C”, “D”) and stores them in an array.
2. It creates two R×C arrays:
   – `expected[i][j] = j+1`
   – `marked[i][j] = 0` initially.
3. It reads R records of the form `<label> <k>`. For each record, it finds which row index `i` matches `<label>` and sets `marked[i][k–1] = k`.
4. Finally, it iterates over all cells (i,j). Whenever `expected[i][j] != marked[i][j]`, it prints `<label> <expected[i][j]>` using the letter code for row i.

In short, the program finds and reports which numbered positions in each named row were never “hit” by the input.

Description_Simple:
Title: Traffic Flow Aggregator on a Fixed Grid

Main Goal:
This obfuscated program reads a number of records from standard input, each specifying a direction code (1–4), a quantity, and grid coordinates (row and column). It maintains four separate 3×10 integer matrices—one per direction—and, for each record, adds the specified quantity into the appropriate cell of the matrix matching its direction. After processing all input, it prints out each direction’s matrix in turn (in the order of codes 1 through 4), separating the blocks with decrypted header labels. Utility methods implement simple comparisons, base-64/XOR and DES/MD5 decryption to conceal the direction headers.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program manages four separate 2D tables (each 3 × 10 in size). First it reads an integer N (the number of updates), then reads N lines of the form
   type r c value
where:
 • type ∈ {0,1,2,3} selects which of the four tables to touch,  
 • r,c are 1-based row and column indices (converted internally to 0-based),  
 • value is an integer to add.  

For each update, it simply adds the given value into table[type][r][c].  Once all updates are processed, it prints out the contents of each of the four tables in turn (row by row, columns separated by spaces), with a blank line or header between them.

Description_Simple:
Title: Matrix-Vector Multiplication

Main Goal: The code reads two integers n and m (separated by “$”), then an n×m integer matrix (rows split by spaces), then an m-element integer vector (one per line). It validates dimensions and element ranges (0–1000), computes the product of the matrix by the vector, and prints the resulting n-element vector.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads a matrix–vector multiplication problem from standard input, validates that all dimensions and entries are within the allowed non-negative ranges, performs the multiplication, and prints the resulting vector. Concretely:

1. It reads one line with two integers N and M (number of rows and columns).
2. It then reads N lines, each with M non‐negative integers, building an N×M matrix A.
3. It reads a further M lines, each with one non‐negative integer, forming a length-M vector B.
4. It computes the product C = A × B (an N‐element vector), where  
   C[i] = Σ_{j=0..M–1} A[i][j] * B[j].
5. Finally, it outputs each entry of C on its own line.

All the obfuscation (renamed variables, bogus branches, string encryption, encrypted method/array names, dead code, etc.) merely hides this straightforward matrix-vector multiplication logic.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Student Grade Classifier

Main goal:
This program repeatedly reads three integers (two theory marks and one practical mark) until a triple of zeros is entered. For each input:
- If either theory mark is zero, it prints an “Invalid Marks” message.
- Otherwise, it computes the sum of the two theory marks and, together with the practical mark, classifies the student’s result into one of several categories:
  • Sum ≥ 80: “Distinction”  
  • 65 ≤ Sum < 80: “First Class”  
  • 50 ≤ Sum < 65: “Second Class”  
  • 30 ≤ Sum < 50 and practical ≥ 50: “Pass”  
  • 30 ≤ Sum < 50 and practical < 50: “Supplementary”  
  • Sum < 30: “Fail”

Key functions:
- IIlIIIIlIIl(): initializes all the numeric constants used for comparison.
- llIIIIIlIIl() and IlIIIIIlIIl(): decrypt hard-coded, encrypted message strings at startup using DES and Blowfish.
- Helper methods (IllIIIIlIIl, IIIlIIIlIIl, lIIlIIIlIIl, lIlIIIIlIIl, lllIIIIlIIl) perform simple integer comparison operations.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads lines of three integers (a, b, c) until they are all zero, then exits. For each non‐zero triple it:

1. Computes s = a + b.
2. Always prints the first decrypted message.
3. Tests s against a fixed sequence of intervals:  
   – 2 ≤ s < 6  
   – 6 ≤ s < 12  
   – 12 ≤ s < 16  
   – 16 ≤ s < 20  
   – 20 ≤ s < 24  
   – s ≥ 24  
   Some of these interval tests also require that c meets a minimum threshold (c ≥ 6) before printing.  
4. For each interval that passes its test, it prints the corresponding decrypted string from a static array.

All of the human‐readable output strings are stored in encrypted form (a mix of DES and Blowfish with Base64) and are decrypted exactly once in the static initializer. The control‐flow is heavily obfuscated, but the real logic is simply: loop over input triples, break on three zeros, compute s = a + b, and print one or more fixed messages depending on which numeric ranges s (and, for some messages, c) fall into.

Description_Simple:
Title: Greedy Triple-Packing Counter

Main Goal:
This program reads multiple test cases (pairs of integers N and S) from standard input until it encounters “0 0.” For each case it counts, using a simple greedy algorithm, how many distinct triples (i, j, k) with 1 ≤ i < j < k ≤ N and i+j+k = S can be selected so that no two chosen triples share any pair of numbers. It then prints one count per line for all test cases.

Key Steps:
1. Decrypts a single hidden string (“ ”) via a Blowfish/MD5 routine to use as the input‐split delimiter.
2. Reads lines, splits on space, parses N and S.
3. If (N, S) = (0, 0) → stop and output accumulated results.
4. If S < 3 → record 0 (no triples possible).
5. Otherwise, enumerate all i<j<k ≤ N with sum S;
   – in lex order, add a triple only if it shares at most one element (i.e. no pair) with any already chosen triple.
   – maintain a running list of accepted triples.
   – after scanning, record the size of that list.
6. After all cases, print each recorded count on its own line.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads pairs of integers N and K (one pair per line, space-separated) until it encounters “0 0.” For each (N,K) it computes how many distinct 3-element combinations {i,j,ℓ} with 1 ≤ i < j < ℓ ≤ N have i + j + ℓ = K. If K is smaller than the minimum possible sum (1+2+3=6), it immediately records 0. Otherwise it uses three nested loops over i, j, ℓ (with i<j<ℓ) to count every triple summing to K. After processing all cases, it prints one result per line in the same order.

Description_Simple:

Main Goal: This program reads an M×N matrix from standard input, computes the sum of each row and appends it as a new last column, computes the sum of each column and prints it as a new last row, and finally fills the bottom-right corner with the overall sum of all elements. It then outputs the resulting (M+1)×(N+1) augmented matrix.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads two integers n and m, then reads an n×m grid of integers. It builds an (n+1)×(m+1) table that augments the original grid with:

1. An extra column at index m holding each row’s sum.
2. An extra row at index n holding each column’s sum.
3. The bottom‐right cell (row n, column m) set to half of the total sum of all input numbers.

Finally, it prints out this extended table: each of the first n rows prints its m values followed by the row sum, and then the final row prints the m column sums and the half‐total in the last cell.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Matrix Multiplication Program  
Main Goal: This heavily obfuscated Java code reads three integers (n, m, p), then reads an n×m matrix and an m×p matrix from standard input, validates the dimensions, computes their matrix product, and prints each resulting row either as concatenated numbers or space-separated entries depending on a flag.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The obfuscated program is simply a matrix‐multiplication utility with bounds checking. At start it reads a line of four values (row count R, some ignored token, column count C, and inner‐dimension count K), validates that R and C and K lie within configured bounds, then:

1. Reads R lines each containing C non‐negative integers (matrix A), rejecting any out‐of‐range entry.
2. Reads C lines each containing K non‐negative integers (matrix B), likewise rejecting invalid entries.
3. Computes the standard product A × B to produce an R × K result matrix.
4. Prints each of the R result rows as space‐separated long integers.

All the convoluted jumps, dead code, renamed variables, and encrypted strings serve only to obscure these straightforward steps.

Description_Simple:
Title: Encrypted String Initializer and Custom Text Decoder

Main Goal: This Java program first decrypts and initializes a small set of hidden strings (using Base64+DES, Base64+Blowfish, and a custom XOR routine). It then reads a line of user input, splits it on a secret delimiter, and for each character of each segment decides—based on its presence in one of three secret alphabets—which alphabet to copy it from. The result is a reconstructed output string that is only printed if its length stays under a predefined threshold.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads one line of text from standard input, splits it on a fixed delimiter, and then “decodes” each token by performing a simple character‐substitution between two hard-coded alphabets. For each character in each token it checks whether the character appears only in alphabet A, only in alphabet B, or in both. If it’s in A alone, it replaces it with the character at the same index in B; if it’s in B alone, it replaces it with the character at the same index in A; if it’s in both, it leaves it unchanged. It reassembles the tokens (inserting spaces between them) and, if the total length of the input tokens stays below a preset threshold, prints out the resulting decoded string. All the surrounding jumps, fake branches, encrypted literals, and extra variables are just obfuscation; the true function is a straightforward bidirectional substitution cipher decoder with a length check.

Description_Simple: This heavily obfuscated Java program defines helper methods to build an array of integer constants (ASCII codes for '1'–'9', plus some others) and to decrypt a single Base64-encoded DES block to recover a secret sentinel string. In main(), it reads lines from standard input in a loop, checks each line against the decrypted sentinel, and breaks if they match. Otherwise it walks through each character of the line, and whenever it encounters the characters '1' through '9' (using the obfuscated ASCII constants), it adds the corresponding numeric value (1–9) to an accumulator. After scanning the whole line it prints the total sum of those digits. The program terminates only when the special secret keyword is entered.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program repeatedly reads lines of text from standard input until it sees a special “exit” keyword (the exact word is stored encrypted in the code). For each non-exit line, it scans each character and, whenever it encounters one of the digit characters ‘1’ through ‘9’, adds that digit’s numeric value to a running total. At the end of the line it prints the sum of all digits in that line, then loops back for the next input line. When the user finally types the exit keyword, the program terminates.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Input Checker with Encrypted Messages

Main goal: This heavily-obfuscated Java program reads a single integer from standard input, compares it to a hidden “key” value, and then prints one of two secret messages (decrypted at runtime) depending on whether the input matches that key. 2. If `x` equals a built-in constant:
     – Print the “success” message.
3. Otherwise:
     – Print the “failure” message.

All of the messages themselves are stored encrypted in string tables and are decrypted by small AES/Blowfish/DES helper routines. There is also an unused `sort` method for long arrays and lots of anti-decompilation cruft.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program consists of two pieces:

1. A tiny “Main” application  
   - It uses a custom fast‐reader (named `Foster`) to read a single integer from standard input.  
   - Internally, it holds one precomputed threshold constant (loaded via a static obfuscated initializer).  
   - At runtime it decrypts two fixed messages (once at class‐load time, via AES/DES/Blowfish and XOR/Base64 routines).  
   - In `main()` it checks whether the input integer meets or exceeds that threshold.  
     - If so, it prints the first decrypted message.  
     - Otherwise, it prints the second decrypted message.  
   - There is also a helper method `sort(long[])` that converts a `long` array into an `ArrayList<Long>`, sorts it in ascending order, and writes the results back into the original array. This sorting routine is defined but never used by `main()`.

Description_Detailed:

4. Otherwise, it initializes a running product `P` with the smallest value.
5. It then iterates through the rest of the sorted array (from smallest to largest), and for each element `x`:
   - If multiplying `P` by `x` would stay within the hard limit `10^18`, it updates `P *= x`.
   - If it would exceed `10^18`, it stops and records failure.
6. After processing all elements:
   - If all multiplications succeeded without overflow, it prints the final product `P`.
   - If it stopped early because of the overflow check, it prints `-1`.
7. Finally, it flushes the output.

In short, the code computes the product of the array’s elements in ascending order (starting from the smallest), stopping with `-1` if the partial product ever exceeds `10^18`, or printing the product (or `0` if any element is zero).

3.  remaining_after_b = max(remaining_after_a − b, 0)

5.  result = filled − subtract_c  

Finally it prints result.

In other words, you “fill” up to d units from a, “skip” b units, then “remove” up to c of the leftover capacity, and output how many units remain from the original fill.

Description_Simple:
Title: Maximizing Active Units in Work‐Rest Cycles

Main goal: Read three integers X, A and B, then compute 
  result = (X / (A + B)) * A + min(A, X % (A + B)), 
i.e. the maximum “active” (A-length) units you can fit into a total of X units when each cycle consists of A active units followed by B rest units. FastScanner is just a fast input utility.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The program reads three 64-bit integers x, a, and b. It views x as a total supply to be allocated in “blocks” of size (a + b), where each full block yields a contribution of size a. It computes the number of full blocks t = floor(x / (a + b)), so the partial result is t × a. It then looks at the remainder r = x – t ×(a + b). If r < a, it adds r; otherwise it adds a. Finally it prints the total:  
   result = t·a + min(r, a)  
In other words, from x units you take as many full (a+b) blocks as you can (gaining a units per block) and then you get up to a more units from the leftover, but not exceeding a.

    M ≤ 0.1·k  ≤ M+1   ⇒   k ∈ [ceil(M/0.1),  floor((M+1)/0.1)]  
Those bounds are carefully computed in floating‐point then adjusted to account for exact integers.  Finally, it checks for an overlapping k in the two ranges.  If a common k exists it prints that k, otherwise it prints “-1” (decoded via a Base64+XOR obfuscation routine).   floor(0.08 × X) = A  
  floor(0.10 × X) = B

Equivalently,  
  A/0.08 ≤ X < (A+1)/0.08  
  B/0.10 ≤ X < (B+1)/0.10.  

It computes the two intervals by taking appropriate ceil and floor bounds, intersects them, and then:

– If exactly one integer lies in the overlap, it prints that integer.  
– If the overlap contains more than one integer, it prints the lower (or upper, according to which branch matches) bound of the intersection.  
– If there is no overlap at all, it prints a predefined message (e.g. “impossible” or “-1”).

In short, given percentages A% = floor(8X/100) and B% = floor(10X/100), it recovers X when possible, reports ambiguity if there are multiple solutions, and signals failure if there is none.

Description_Simple:
Title: Computing the Smallest Mersenne Number ≥ N

Main Goal:
This program reads a single long integer N from standard input and computes the smallest integer of the form (2^k – 1) that is greater than or equal to N. It then prints that value.

How it works:
1. It stores a memoization map with the base case f(1)=1.
2. Defines a recursive function dfs(x):
   - If x is already in the map, return its value.
   - Otherwise compute dfs(x/2), double it, add 1, store in the map, and return it.
3. Because dfs(x)=2·dfs(⌊x/2⌋)+1 with dfs(1)=1, one can show by induction that dfs(N)=2^{⌊log₂N⌋+1}–1.
4. In solve(), it reads N, initializes the map, and prints dfs(N).

All other methods (gcd, lcm, scanner utilities, cryptographic imports) are boilerplate or unused in the core logic.

The program reads a single long integer N from standard input and prints a number of the form 2^k – 1, where k is one plus the index of the highest set‐bit in N (i.e. k = ⌊log2 N⌋+1). Concretely, it finds the greatest power of two ≤ N (call it 2^h) and outputs 2^(h+1)−1 (for example N=13 ⇒ h=3 ⇒ output=15, N=16 ⇒ h=4 ⇒ output=31). Internally this is done by a simple memoized recursive routine dfs(x): 
    – dfs(1)=1  
    – dfs(x)=2·dfs(x/2)+1  
and a HashMap cache, but all the fancy renaming, dead‐code, control‐flow tricks, and string­-encryption support code around Input/Output are purely obfuscation layers and do not affect the core computation.

Description_Detailed:

1. If A ≥ C:
     A ← A – C;  B unchanged  
2. Otherwise:
     Crem ← C – A  
     A ← 0  
     B ← max(0, B – Crem)

Then output A and B.

Description_Simple:

Description_Detailed:

  • Converts the resulting indices back to letters (A→0, B→1, …, Z→25) and prints them.

In effect, it takes a lowercase word, shifts each letter forward by N positions in the alphabet (wrapping around), and outputs the result in uppercase.

Description_Simple:

   - If 1 ≤ N ≤ 9  
   - Else if N is divisible by 2 and 2 ≤ N ≤ 18  
   - Else if N is divisible by 3 and 3 ≤ N ≤ 31

The `solve()` method picks the right decrypted string for the first matching bucket and returns it.  Finally, `main()` prints that string.

All of the complicated alphabet soup (fake variables, bogus jumps, string‐decryption methods, unused code blocks, etc.) is just obfuscation around this core logic of “classify N by simple range-and-divisibility tests, then look up and print one of ten predetermined messages.”

Description_Simple:

Summary Description:
 The program reads a single long integer N from standard input. It initializes the best answer to N−1 (which corresponds to the trivial factor pair 1 and N). Then it loops i from 1 up to ⌊√N⌋. Whenever i divides N exactly, it computes the complementary factor j = N/i and considers the value (i−1)+(j−1). If this is smaller than the current best, it updates the best. After the loop it prints the minimum found, which equals min_{a·b=N}(a+b−2). A custom FastReader handles input efficiently, and several tiny comparison helper methods hide the straightforward divisor-search logic.
Description_Detailed:

This program reads a single long integer N from standard input, then factors N by testing every i from 1 up to √N.  Whenever it finds a divisor i (so that j = N/i is integral), it computes the quantity (i + j − 2).  It keeps track of the minimum of these values over all divisor pairs and, after the loop, prints that minimum.  In effect, it finds the factor pair of N whose sum is smallest, subtracts 2, and outputs the result.

Description_Simple:

 (sum of all elements)² – (sum of squares)  
divided by 2, it outputs

which equals the sum of A[i] * A[j] over all 0 ≤ i < j < N. The rest of the code provides a fast input reader and some decompiled boilerplate.
Description_Detailed:

    (S² − Q) / 2

which algebraically equals ∑_{0≤i<j<N} a[i]·a[j]. In other words, it efficiently computes the sum of all pairwise products a[i]·a[j] for i<j.

In essence, this is an obfuscated CLI that recognizes two secret commands and prints back two secret messages, all of which are stored encrypted in the code.

Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>

Description_Simple: This Java program uses a custom fast I/O template to read two long integers, \(x\) and \(y\). Description_Simple:

In short, the code transforms the input array into an output of length n, filling all positions with the global maximum except that if the maximum is unique, at that unique‐max position it prints the largest of the other values (special‐casing n = 2 & max at index 0).

   D = ∑_{k=0..M-1} (A[i][k] – A[j][k])².
4. Check whether √D is an exact integer (i.e. D is a perfect square).
5. Count how many pairs (i, j) satisfy that their distance is an integer.
