Main goal: This obfuscated Java program reads a single input string and checks for any two identical characters in a row. If it finds a repeated character pair, it prints “Bad” and exits; otherwise it prints “Good.”
Description_Detailed: The program reads a single token (a “word”) from standard input and scans it left to right looking for any two identical characters in a row.  As soon as it finds a pair of equal adjacent characters it prints the first (failure) message and exits; if it gets to the end without finding any, it prints the second (success) message. All of the convoluted branching, dead‐code and encrypted strings are just hiding that simple check for consecutive equal letters.

Description_Simple:
Title: Maximum Sum of an Arithmetic Sequence Excluding the Smallest Absolute Value Element

Main Goal: Given two integers n and k, the code constructs the arithmetic sequence k, k+1, …, k+n–1 and computes the sum of all its elements except the one with the smallest absolute value. This effectively maximizes the total sum by omitting the term closest to zero (or zero itself, if present).

Key Steps and Functions:
1. Read pairs of integers (n, k) until end of input.
2. Build the array arr[i] = k + i for i = 0…n–1.
3. Determine the sign distribution of the sequence’s endpoints:
   - If all terms are negative: sum elements from index 0 to n–2.
   - If all terms are positive or start at zero: sum elements from index 1 to n–1.
   - If the sequence crosses zero: sum all nonzero elements (skipping the single zero).
4. Print the resulting sum for each input pair.

Helper Boolean Methods:
- llIIIIIllll(n, m): returns n < m
- IlIIIIIllll(n): returns n != 0
- lIlIIIIllll(n): returns n == 0
- IIlIIIIllll(n): returns n < 0
- IllIIIIllll(n): returns n <= 0
- lllIIIIllll(n): returns n > 0
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program repeatedly reads pairs of integers n and x from standard input until EOF. It forms the length-n arithmetic sequence a[i] = x + i for i=0…n–1, then computes the sum of all its terms except the one whose absolute value is smallest:

• If the entire sequence is negative (x + n–1 < 0), it skips the last term (closest to zero).  
• If the entire sequence is positive (x > 0), it skips the first term (closest to zero).  
• If the sequence crosses zero (x < 0 and x + n–1 > 0), it skips the term equal to zero (i.e. when x + i = 0).

Finally it prints that adjusted sum and loops for the next (n, x) pair.

Description_Simple:
Title: Counting Numbers in a Range Excluding Multiples of Two Divisors

Main Goal:
Given four long integers A, B, X, Y, the code computes how many integers in the inclusive interval [A, B] are not divisible by X or by Y.

Description:
1. Reads A, B, X, Y from standard input.
2. Computes L = lcm(X, Y) via gcd.
3. Uses inclusion–exclusion:
   - Total numbers = B–A+1
   - Subtract count of multiples of X in [A,B]
   - Subtract count of multiples of Y in [A,B]
   - Add back count of multiples of L in [A,B]
4. Prints the result.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads four long integers A, B, C, D. It then computes L = lcm(C, D) via gcd. Finally, it outputs the count of integers in the inclusive range [A..B] that are _not_ divisible by C _and_ _not_ divisible by D. Internally it handles three cases:

1. A == B (single number): it checks that this one value is not a multiple of C nor D and prints 1 if so, else 0.
2. C == D (only one “forbidden” divisor): it computes the total length (B-A+1) minus the number of multiples of C in [A..B].
3. General case (two distinct divisors): it applies inclusion–exclusion:
   – count C = multiples of C in [A..B]  
   – count D = multiples of D  
   – count L = multiples of LCM(C,D)  
   – result = (B–A+1) – count C – count D + count L  

and prints that.

Description_Simple: This Java program reads two integers n and m, then reads an array of n integers. It keeps a running sum from the first element onward and counts how many elements are needed before that sum becomes greater than m. Once the running total exceeds m, it prints the count of elements processed. The code uses an obfuscated FastScanner class for fast input parsing.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads two integers N and X, then an array A of N integers. It scans the array from the start, accumulating a running sum S. As soon as S exceeds X, it stops and prints the 1-based count of elements used (i.e. the length of the shortest prefix whose sum is > X). All the surrounding code is just the usual fast-Input/Output scaffolding (with many fake branches, encrypted strings, renamed variables, etc.)—the real algorithm is simply “find the first prefix whose sum exceeds X and output its length.”

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Java Program for Computing Half‐Product and Validation

Main Goal:
This code reads two double values a and b, and two integers c and d, computes the “area” defined as a*b/2, and then checks whether a and b are exactly twice c and d, respectively (i.e. 2*c==a and 2*d==b). It prints the computed half‐product followed by one of two hidden strings (decrypted at runtime, effectively “YES” or “NO”) depending on that equality test. The rest of the code consists of an obfuscated FastScanner for input and encrypted string constants that are decrypted with Blowfish/DES.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>  
The program reads four values from standard input: two doubles A and B, and then two integers X and Y. It computes the triangle‐area D = A * B / 2.0. Next it checks whether X and Y are large enough so that 2·X ≥ A and 2·Y ≥ B. If both conditions hold, it prints the area D followed by one decrypted label (e.g. “YES”); otherwise it prints D followed by the other decrypted label (e.g. “NO”). In other words, it reports the half‐rectangle area and whether the given integer bounds X, Y suffice to cover the full dimensions A, B.

Description_Simple:
This decompiled and heavily obfuscated Java code defines a Main class that, on startup, decrypts a set of string constants (using Blowfish, XOR-based Base64, DES and AES with MD5‐derived keys). In its main method it reads exactly one integer, checks whether it equals a secret threshold (stored in an encrypted integer array), and then prints one of two secret messages (also decrypted at startup). Beyond this central input–compare–print flow, it provides:
 • A static sort(long[]) method that wraps a long[] in an ArrayList, calls Collections.sort, and writes back the sorted values.
 • Cryptographic helper methods (lllIlll, Illllll, llIlIIIl, IIIlIll) that implement Blowfish, XOR‐Base64, DES and AES decryption.
 • A decompiled InputReader for reading tokens, ints, and longs.
 • A trivial Point class that holds two integers.
All constant values and control‐flow (comparisons, array indices) have been buried under layers of bitwise and length‐of‐string checks to foil straightforward analysis.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The de-obfuscated program is essentially a tiny template that:

1. Reads a single integer N from standard input.  
2. Compares N against a hard-coded threshold (decrypted from the static data).  
3. If N is at least that threshold, it prints one decrypted string (e.g. “YES”); otherwise it prints the other (e.g. “NO”).  
4. All of the apparent complexity—encryption routines, meaningless branches, unused loops, the long array sorter, the Point class and custom InputReader/OutputWriter—is purely boilerplate or dead code.  The real runtime behavior is nothing more than “read an int, compare it, and print one of two constant messages.”

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Matrix Multiplication with Input Validation

Main Goal: This Java program reads three integers n, m, k (all in the range 1…100), then reads two matrices A (n×m) and B (m×k) with non-negative entries up to 10 000. It validates the dimensions and element bounds, computes the product matrix C = A×B (size n×k), and prints each row of C with space-separated values.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads three integers N, M, P from standard input, then reads an N×M matrix followed by an M×P matrix (all entries are non-negative and ≤10 000, with N, M, P in the range [1,100]). It verifies these bounds, and if they pass, computes the N×P product C = A×B in the usual way:

for each i in 0…N−1 and j in 0…P−1:
 C[i][j] = Σₖ₌₀…M−1 A[i][k]×B[k][j].

Finally it prints the resulting N rows of P numbers, space-separated.

Description_Simple:
Title: Climbing Stairs with Broken Rungs (Dynamic Programming)

Main Goal:
This obfuscated Java program reads two integers, N (the total number of rungs) and M (the number of broken rungs), then reads the M distinct broken‐rung positions. If any two broken rungs are consecutive, it decrypts and prints a stored error message. Otherwise it uses a Fibonacci-style DP (modulo 1 000 000 007) to count the number of ways to climb from the bottom (rung 0) to the top (rung N), taking 1‐ or 2‐rung steps and never landing on a broken rung. The final count is printed to standard output.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>

This program reads two integers, N and M, then reads M distinct “blocked” positions (each input minus one) into an array. It constructs an integer sequence F of length N as follows:

1. Initialize an index pointer p = 0.
2. For each i from 0 to N–1:
   - If i matches the next blocked position arr[p], mark F[i] = –1 and advance p.
   - Otherwise mark F[i] = 0.
3. If N ≥ 1, set the first element F[0] = 1.
4. If N ≥ 2, choose F[1] = 1 or 0 depending on whether position 1 is blocked.
5. For i from 2 to N–1:
   - If F[i] was marked –1 (i.e. a blocked index), compute F[i] = (F[i–1] + F[i–2]) mod MOD.
   - Otherwise leave F[i] = 0.

Here MOD is a large constant hard-coded in the static initializer. Finally it computes X = F[N–1] mod MOD. If X==0 it prints a fixed decrypted message (“oajQI”→“You’re awesome!”), otherwise it prints the integer X.

In effect, the code treats the input positions as “active” spots where it builds a Fibonacci-like sequence modulo MOD; all other positions stay zero. It outputs the Nth term (1-based) of that modified Fibonacci sequence, or a congratulatory string if that term is zero.

Description_Simple:
Title: Conditional Integer Transformer with Fast Input

Main Goal: This program reads two integers (a and b) from standard input using a custom fast I/O class (FS). It then applies these rules:
- If a ≤ 5, set b = 0.
- Else if a ≤ 12, replace b with b / 2 (integer division).
- Otherwise leave b unchanged.
Finally, it prints the resulting value of b.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads two integers, x and y, from standard input and prints a single integer result based on x:

1. If x ≤ 5, it ignores the original y and prints 0.
2. Else if x ≤ 12, it divides y by 2 (integer division) and prints that.
3. Otherwise (x > 12) it simply prints y unchanged.

All of the obfuscated code outside of these checks—fake jumps, dead branches, weird string operations, encrypted literals, renamed variables, etc.—serves only to hide this straightforward logic.

Description_Simple:
Title: Computing the Length of the Common Overlap of M Intervals

Main Goal:
 Given an integer N (the initial allowable range [0…N]) and M closed intervals, the code reads all M intervals and computes the size (number of integer points) in the intersection of all those intervals. If the M intervals have no point in common, it outputs 0.

Summary Description:
 The program first de-obfuscates two constants:  
  • ZERO = 0  
  • ONE  = 1  

 It then reads two integers:  
  • N – defines the initial interval [0, N]  
  • M – the number of intervals to process  

 If M == 1, it reads a single interval [L,R] and immediately prints R–L+1.  
 Otherwise it initializes a “current overlap” to [start=0, end=N] and iterates over the M input intervals [L,R]. On each step it replaces the current overlap with its intersection with [L,R]:  
  • newStart = max(oldStart, L)  
  • newEnd   = min(oldEnd,   R)  

 After each update it recomputes the length = newEnd – newStart + 1.  
 If at any point the intervals do not overlap, it breaks out and will print 0.  
 Finally it prints the size of the intersection of all M intervals.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The program reads two integers, n and m. It then reads m pairs of integers, each pair (a, b) defining a closed interval [a, b] on the integer line. Treating an initial “allowed” range of [0, n], it successively intersects that range with each of the m input intervals. After each step it updates the current intersection to the overlap of the previous intersection with the new interval; if at any point there is no overlap, it immediately sets the result to 0 and stops processing further intervals. Finally, it prints the size (number of integer points) of the final intersection, i.e. max(0, end – start + 1). If m happens to be 1, it skips the general loop and directly outputs b – a + 1 for that single interval.

Description_Simple: The Main class uses an obfuscated static array llIIIIIll holding [1, 32]. It reads two integers (the first unused, the second used as a 1-based index) and a string. It converts the string to a char array, computes zero-based index = position–1, then does char[index] = (char)(char[index] + 32). This shifts the ASCII code of that character by 32 (e.g. 'A'→'a'), rebuilds the string, and prints it. The FastScanner class is a heavily obfuscated I/O utility for tokenized input (next(), nextInt(), nextLong(), etc.).
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads three inputs from standard input:

1. An integer (which it actually ignores in the rest of its logic),  
2. A second integer k,  
3. A string s.

It then converts s to a character array, locates the character at position k – 1, increases its Unicode code‐point by 32, writes that modified character back into the array, reconstructs the string, and prints it.  

In practice, adding 32 to an ASCII letter will turn an uppercase letter into its lowercase counterpart (e.g. 'A'→'a'), so the program effectively lowercases the k-th character of the input string (1-based index) and leaves the rest of the string unchanged. The supporting `FastScanner` class is simply a fast I/O utility.

Description_Simple: An obfuscated Java program that hides all its string constants (error messages, regex patterns, valid and invalid codes) in encrypted form (Base64+XOR, DES, Blowfish). At startup it decrypts them into an array, then in main() it reads a single two‐character token, splits it into the first and second character, ensures each matches a compiled regex, tests each against hardcoded allow/deny lists, and prints one of four possible status messages (both valid, first only, second only, neither) or an overall failure message if they don’t match the regex. The two helper functions perform XOR+Base64 decoding and DES/Blowfish decryption to recover the constants.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads a single string token from standard input, splits it into two one‐character substrings (the “first” and “second” characters), and then:

1. Verifies that both characters match a predefined regular‐expression pattern (in the shipped code, a digit‐pattern).
2. For each character, tests membership in a hard‐coded set of allowed characters by comparing against a list of literal strings (decrypted at class‐load time).
3. Based on whether each character belongs to its respective set, it prints exactly one of four possible messages:
   – both characters in their sets  
   – first in, second out  
   – first out, second in  
   – both out  
4. If either character fails the regex check, it prints an “invalid input” message.

All of the surrounding gotos, dummy branches, bogus variables, encrypted literals, and cipher routines exist only to hide this simple “two‐character classification → one-of‐four outputs (or error)” logic.

Description_Simple:
Title: Average of Raised Powers Based on Doubling Steps

Main Goal:
This program (in its active routine solveC) reads two integers N and M, and for each starting value i=1..N computes the minimum number of times t you must double i (i → 2·i → 4·i → …) before it reaches or exceeds M.  It then raises a fixed base B (loaded from an obfuscated constant) to that power t, sums those B^t values for all i, and finally outputs the average 
   (Σ_{i=1..N} B^{t_i}) ÷ N 
as a BigDecimal with a fixed number of decimal places.  

Support code:
– A fully in-house fast input reader (hasNext, nextInt, next(), etc.)  
– Several swap-free comparison helpers (lIIllIIIIIIl, IlIllIIIIIIl, …)  
– Static routines to decrypt and assemble the string constants used for output messages and the base B.  

Only the solveC method is actually invoked by main; solveA..solveF are unused stubs for other problems.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program’s real work is in the `solveC()` method. It reads two integers, N and M, and then for each i from 1 up to N–1 computes the smallest non‐negative integer t such that  
  i·2ᵗ ≥ M  
(i.e. how many times you must “double” i before reaching or exceeding M). It then takes 10ᵗ, sums those values over all i, divides the total by N to form an average, and prints that average as a BigDecimal rounded to 7 decimal places. All of the weird branches, dead code, encrypted strings, and fake methods merely obscure this straightforward calculation.

Description_Simple:
Title: Block-Based Cost Calculator

Main goal: Read three integers A, B, and C, then compute how many increments of size A are needed to exceed C and output the total cost as that count multiplied by B.

Description: The program uses a custom FastScanner to read A (block size), B (cost per block), and C (target value). It initializes an accumulator to A and a cost counter to 0. While the accumulator is less than or equal to C, it adds another block (accumulator += A) and increases the cost by B. Once the accumulator exceeds C, it prints the accumulated cost.
Description_Detailed:
This program reads three integers from standard input: A, B, and C. It then initializes two running values:

 • A floating‐point sum S, starting at S = A  
 • An integer accumulator X, starting at a fixed offset X = 4  

It repeatedly does the following until S ≥ C + 0.5:
 1. Add A to S  
 2. Add B to X  

When the loop exits, it prints X.

In other words, it counts how many times you must add A to itself before exceeding (C + 0.5), multiplies that count by B, adds the constant 4, and outputs the result.

Description_Simple:
Title: Sum of Positive Differences between Two Arrays

Main Goal: This program reads an integer N, then reads two integer sequences A and B of length N each. It computes and prints the total sum of (A[i] – B[i]) only for those indices i where A[i] > B[i].

Explanation:
- Uses a custom InputReader for fast input and OutputWriter for output.
- The unused `round` function rounds a double to a given number of decimal places.
- In `main`, after reading N, it fills arrays A and B.
- It then iterates over all positions, accumulating (A[i]–B[i]) whenever A[i] exceeds B[i].
- Finally, it outputs the accumulated sum as a long integer.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>  
This program reads an integer N, then reads two sequences of N integers (let’s call them A[0…N−1] and B[0…N−1]). It computes the total of all positive differences A[i]−B[i] (i.e. for each i, if A[i] > B[i], add A[i]−B[i] to a running sum; otherwise add zero). Finally, it prints that sum. The extra methods (rounding, encrypted strings, dead‐code branches, renamed variables, etc.) and the custom fast I/O classes are all just obfuscation—none of that alters the core logic described above.

Description_Simple:
Title: AtCoder Problem Solver (Simple Conditional Sum)

Main Goal: 
This program reads two integers A and B. If A equals B, it outputs their sum (A + B). Otherwise, it outputs (2 × max(A, B) – 1). It uses a custom FastScanner for input and PrintWriter for output, following a typical competitive‐programming template.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The program reads two integers A and B from standard input and writes a single integer result according to these rules:

1. If A == B, it prints A + B.
2. If A > B, it prints 2·A − 1.
3. Otherwise (B > A), it prints 2·B − 1.

All the surrounding complexity (weird jumps, dummy code, encrypted strings, renamed variables) only obscures this simple conditional‐print logic, and the FastScanner class is just a custom input reader for tokens, ints, longs, and doubles.

Description_Simple:
Title: Counting Record-Breaking Array Elements

Main goal: Read an integer N, then N more integers from standard input; scan the array while maintaining the current maximum and count how many times an element is at least as large as any previously seen value (including the first element). Finally, print that count. The code uses a custom fast I/O helper class for input parsing.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>  
The obfuscated program simply reads an integer N, then reads N more integers into an array. It then scans the array from left to right, tracking the running maximum. It initializes a count to 1 (for the first element) and “current max” to the first array value. For each subsequent element, if that element is greater than or equal to the running maximum, it increments the count and updates the running maximum. Finally, it prints the count. In other words, it counts how many times an element sets a new (non‐strict) record high as you walk through the list. The rest of the code is just a custom fast I/O class, and the cryptic static fields and helper methods are all part of the obfuscation.

Description_Simple:
Title: Counting Bounded Integer Triples Summing to S

Main goal: Given two integers K and S, the code computes the number of non-negative integer triples (x, y, z) with x + y + z = S and 0 ≤ x, y, z ≤ K. It does this by:
- f(t, K): counting the number of pairs (x, y) with x + y = t and 0 ≤ x, y ≤ K.
- g(S, K): summing f(S – z, K) over z = 0…K to cover all possible third‐variable choices.
The result is printed to standard output.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The program reads two integers K and S from standard input, and computes the number of non‐negative integer solutions (x, y, z), each ≤ K, such that x + y + z = S.  Concretely:

1. f(a, K) returns the number of pairs (y, z) with 0 ≤ y, z ≤ K and y + z = a (zero if a<0 or a>2K).
2. g(S, K) sums f(S – x, K) for x running from 0 to K, thereby counting all triples (x, y, z) in [0,K]^3 with x + y + z = S.

The result g(S, K) is printed.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Integer‐Array Validation and Conditional Message Output

Main goal:
This program reads six integers from standard input, enforces that they are all between 0 and 123, non-decreasing, and that the last two values are equal. It then treats the first five numbers as a sorted list and the sixth as a threshold, checks every pairwise difference among the first five against that threshold, and finally prints one of two messages (both stored in obfuscated form and decrypted at runtime) indicating either “failure” or “success.”
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads exactly six integers from standard input (re-prompting until all six satisfy the simple validity checks: each must be ≥0, ≤ a fixed upper bound, and the sequence must be non-decreasing). Once a valid six-element array is obtained, it examines every pair of entries i<j and computes the difference arr[j]−arr[i]. If any of those differences exceeds the value of the last element in the array, it immediately prints a first decrypted message (e.g. “NO” or “Error”) and quits. If it finishes all pairwise checks without finding an excessive difference, it prints a second decrypted message (e.g. “YES” or “OK”). The obfuscated parts are just string encryption routines, fake branches, and renamed helpers; the core logic is this simple range-and-ordering validation plus pairwise-difference check with two possible outputs.

Description_Simple:
Title: Container Capacity Optimization

Main Goal: This program reads exactly five integer item‐sizes, assigns each item to the smallest “bucket” or container whose capacity meets or exceeds the item size (the buckets have fixed capacities 10, 20, 30, 50, 80, … up to a set of predefined thresholds), sums the total capacity of those chosen buckets, then subtracts the largest single unused space (slack) among all buckets to minimize the overall wasted capacity, and finally prints the optimized total.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads a fixed number (5) of integers from standard input, each representing the size of an item to pack into containers. It has a hard-coded list of container capacity “brackets” (e.g. 18, 40, 50, 62, … – a total of 14 possible capacities). For each item, it picks the smallest container capacity that is ≥ the item’s size and records how much space remains in that container (the leftover). It sums the capacities of all chosen containers, but at the end it subtracts the unused space of the single container that had the largest leftover (i.e. it “reclaims” the biggest waste). Finally it prints this adjusted total capacity. In effect, it computes the minimal total capacity required to hold all five items, allowing you to not pay for the largest unused margin in one container.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Substring Extractor with Runtime-Decrypted Constants

Main goal: This heavily-obfuscated program reads a single token from standard input, decrypts a set of hidden string constants (using Base64, XOR, Blowfish and DES routines), and then scans the user’s input to identify and print the longest contiguous substring whose characters fall within certain decrypted bounds (for example digit or letter ranges). Depending on the input’s overall validity and the length of the found segment, it either prints that longest valid segment, the original input, or a fallback string. All of the index tables and textual literals are concealed in static int and String arrays and are only revealed at runtime by the decryption methods.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>  
This obfuscated program boils down to three things:

1. Static setup  
   – On class load it builds two small static lookup tables:  
     • A secret “pattern” string and a few integer constants, by decrypting several Base64‐XOR and Blowfish/DES blobs.  
     • An empty integer array for result tracking.  

2. Main logic (in Main.main)  
   – It reads exactly one token (a “word”) from standard input.  
   – It extracts four specific characters from the secret pattern string (call them c0,c1,c2,c3).  
   – It then scans all substrings of the input word, looking for the longest contiguous span where every character x satisfies  
        c0 ≤ x ≤ c1  AND  x ≤ c2  AND  x > c3  
     (i.e. x stays within a narrow range defined by those four bounds).  
   – It keeps track of the maximum valid substring length found.  

   – After scanning, it has three possible outputs:  
     a) If the maximum length > 1, it prints that length.  
     b) Else if no multi‐character run was found but there is at least one invalid character, it prints the (1-based) index of the first invalid character.  
     c) Otherwise (the entire word is valid but length ≤1, or all chars satisfy the bounds), it just echoes the original input back.  

3. A helper Pair class  
   – Implements a simple (x,y) pair with equals, hashCode, and toString, all heavily obfuscated but functionally trivial.  

In short, the real algorithm decrypts a hidden 4-character rule, then finds and reports the longest substring of the user’s input whose letters all lie between those four boundaries, or falls back to reporting the first violation or echoing the input.

Description_Simple:
Title: Counting “AC” substrings and simulating health attacks (decompiled AtCoder solution)

Main goal:
1. The Main class reads an integer N (string length), Q (number of queries), and a string S. It preprocesses S to build a prefix‐sum array of the number of times the substring “AC” occurs ending at each position. Then for each query [L, R], it answers in O(1) how many “AC” substrings lie entirely within S[L..R].
2. The AtCoder class solves another problem: it reads an initial health H, an array of N damage values A[i], then simulates subtracting each A[i] in order, printing “No” and stopping if health ≤ 0 at any point, or printing “Yes” if H stays positive after all attacks.
3. The FastScanner class provides a highly‐obfuscated, fast input reader and utility decryption methods (MD5+DES/Blowfish/xor) to decode obfuscated string constants.

Key functions:
- In Main: building the prefix count of “AC” occurrences by scanning adjacent characters, then answering range queries by subtracting prefix sums.
- In AtCoder: a solve() routine that decrements health and checks failure or survival.
- In FastScanner: buffered reading of tokens (next(), nextInt(), nextLong(), etc.) with many helper boolean and decryption routines to hide constant values.
Description_Detailed:
The three classes work together as a tiny “contest‐style” toolkit plus two very simple problem‐solvers:

1) FastScanner is nothing more than a high‐speed stdin reader (next(), nextInt(), etc.) with all of its constants and helper routines buried under heavy encryption and bogus branches.  Once you strip away the obfuscation, it simply reads bytes, skips whitespace, parses integers, longs, doubles, and strings in the usual way.

2) AtCoder is a small solver for the familiar “monster‐health” puzzle: you read an initial health H and then an array A of N positive integers.  You subtract A[0], then A[1], … in order from H.  If at any point H becomes negative or zero you immediately print one of two messages (decrypted from the obfuscated string constants) and stop.  If you manage to subtract all N values and H is still positive, you print the other message.

3) Main solves a simple “range query on a character string” problem.  It reads two integers M (the length of the string) and Q (the number of queries), then a string S of length M split by a single‐character delimiter.  It builds a prefix array P[] so that P[i] counts how many times a particular marker (e.g. a vertical bar ‘|’ or whatever the decrypted literal is) has appeared up to position i.  Then for each query it reads two 1-based indices ℓ and r and prints one of several possible answers computed from:
   – Whether S[ℓ] and S[r] are the special marker or not.
   – The difference P[r] – P[ℓ], sometimes plus or minus one.
   – Or always zero if certain end‐point conditions hold.

   In plain English: it answers “how many of the special symbol occur strictly between ℓ and r, adjusted by whether the endpoints are themselves that symbol or not.”

All of the crazy integer‐array builders, decryption calls, dummy ifs and string‐XOR loops simply disguise the facts that
– FastScanner is a normal fast reader,
– AtCoder does one pass of subtractions checking when health ≤ 0,

Description_Simple:
Title: Positive Weighted Sum Counter

Main Goal:
This program reads three integers N (number of items), M (number of features), and S (initial threshold). It then reads an array of M integer weights. For each of the N items, it reads M feature values, computes the score = S + ∑(weight[j] × feature[j]), and counts how many items produce a positive score. Finally, it prints that count.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The real program (in the `main` method) does the following, ignoring all the obfuscation and unused helper classes:

1. Reads three integers:  
   • n: the number of data rows  
   • m: the length of each row (number of “features”)  
   • k: an initial offset value  

2. Reads an array A of m integer coefficients.

3. Then, for each of the n rows:
   – Reads m integers (call this row X).  
   – Computes the weighted sum S = k + ∑_{j=0..m-1} A[j] * X[j].  
   – If S > 0, increments a counter.

4. After processing all n rows, prints the final counter value.

In short, the program counts how many of the n input vectors X produce a strictly positive result when you take the dot-product with A, add k, and test >0.

Description_Detailed:

Each new digit is compared to the current top of the stack:

At the end it counts how many digits remain in the stack (excluding the initial dummy) and prints the number of digits that were cancelled (i.e. the original length minus the remaining stack size).

Description_Simple:
Title: Threshold Evaluation and Element Filtering

Main goal: Read an integer array, compute a threshold based on the total sum and a given divisor k, count how many elements fall below this threshold, and print “YES” if that count does not exceed k (otherwise “NO”).

Short summary:
1. Read n (array size) and k.
2. Read an array of n integers.
3. Compute the total sum of the array.
4. Calculate threshold = ceil(sum / (4 * k)).
5. Count how many array elements are strictly less than that threshold.
6. If the count of “too small” elements is ≤ k, decrypt and print “YES”; otherwise decrypt and print “NO”.

The code uses an obfuscated Blowfish-based method to store the “YES”/“NO” strings securely, a custom FastScanner for input, and a helper ceil function.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>  
The program reads two integers n and k and then an array a of n positive integers.  It first computes the total sum S of all elements of a.  It then defines a threshold T = ceil(S / (4·k)).  Next it scans the array again and counts how many elements strictly exceed T.  Finally, it compares that count to k and prints one of two fixed messages (“YES”/“NO” in the usual Codeforces style), depending on whether at least k elements are larger than the threshold.  All of the complex-looking code around string decryption, fake branches, gotos and meaningless operations is just obfuscation – the core logic is exactly the simple “count how many a[i] > ceil(sum/(4k)) and check if it is ≥ k.”

Description_Detailed:

It treats the first row (row 0) as special and, for each column index j = 1…M–1, compares G[0][j] against the other rows’ entries in that column.  Whenever G[0][j] exceeds every other row’s value in column j, it counts that column as a “win.”  At the end it prints the total number of winning columns. Description_Simple:
Title: Collatz Sequence Step Counter

Main Goal:
This program reads a single integer N from standard input, then repeatedly applies the Collatz‐map rule—if N is even, divide it by 2; otherwise replace it with 3·N + 1—keeping track of how many steps it takes until any value in the sequence repeats. Finally, it prints the count of steps taken to first encounter a previously seen value (i.e. to enter the cycle).

Summary of Key Components:
1. Obfuscated Constants Initialization  
   - A static array `IlIlIIIIIl` of length 3 is set to {1, 2, 3} via bit‐twiddling (“ ”.length() etc.).

2. Input/Output Setup  
   - `FastScanner sc` for fast reading from `System.in`.  
   - `PrintWriter writer` for writing to `System.out`.

3. Main Loop (in `main`)  
   - Read integer N.  
   - Use a `HashSet<Integer>` to record all past values of N.  
   - Initialize step counter to 0.  
   - While the current N has not been seen before:  
      • Add N to the set, increment the counter.  
      • If N is divisible by 2, set N = N / 2.  
      • Else set N = 3·N + 1.  
   - When a repeat is detected, break and output the step count.

4. FastScanner Class  
   - Custom methods to parse `int`, `long`, `double`, `char`, `String` from `InputStream` using a buffered reader.  
   - Contains several layers of obfuscation (encrypted strings, strange index checks), but functionally just speeds up reading tokens.

Overall, despite heavy decompilation and naming obfuscation, the core algorithm implements the Collatz iteration on an input N and counts how many steps it takes before the sequence cycles.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads a single integer N and then repeatedly applies the classic “3N + 1” (Collatz) rule—if N is even, divide it by 2; otherwise replace N with 3·N + 1—while counting how many steps occur until a previously seen value re-appears. Internally it keeps a HashSet of all values seen so far; once the current N is already in the set (i.e. a cycle has been detected), the loop stops and the step count is printed. All of the obfuscated code around it (weird jumps, bogus methods, encrypted strings, fake variables) simply hides this core Collatz-sequence counter.

Description_Simple:
Title: Minimum Subarray Decrements to Zero

Main goal:
Given an array of non‐negative integers, compute the minimum number of “–1” operations required to turn the entire array into zeros, where each operation selects a contiguous block of positive elements and decrements each element in that block by 1.

How it works:
1. Read n and the array.
2. Loop until all elements are zero:
   a. Scan from left to right, collecting each maximal run of positive numbers.
   b. For each run, use a TreeSet to track its current values and extract the minimum.
   c. Add that minimum to a running total of operations.
   d. Subtract the minimum from every element in the run (ensuring at least one element becomes zero).
   e. Continue scanning for the next run.
3. When no positive elements remain, print the total.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The program reads an integer n and then an array A of n non-negative integers. It computes the minimum number of “segment‐decrement” operations needed to turn the whole array into zeros, where one operation consists of choosing any contiguous subarray whose elements are all positive and subtracting 1 from each of them. Concretely, it repeatedly scans A left to right, breaks it into runs of positive numbers (segments separated by zeros), and for each run:
  1. Finds the minimum value m in the run.
  2. Adds m to a running total (the number of operations).
  3. Subtracts m from every element in that run, which introduces new zeros and may split it further.
It repeats until every element is zero, then prints the total operations. This is the classic “reduce-to-zero-by-subarray-decrements” greedy algorithm (equivalently, summing the minima of the positive segments at each stage).

Description_Simple: This Java program reads an integer N and an array of N integers representing stone heights. It then uses a recursive, memoized dynamic‐programming function to find the least total cost for a frog to move from index 0 to index N−1, where at each step the frog can jump either one or two stones ahead and pays a cost equal to the absolute difference in heights between departure and landing stones. The result is printed to standard output.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The program reads an integer n and then an array H of n integers (heights). It computes, by recursion + memoization, the minimum total “cost” for a frog to go from stone 0 to stone n−1 when in each move it may jump either 1 or 2 stones forward. The cost of a jump from i to j is |H[i]−H[j]|. It stores intermediate results in a DP array to avoid recomputing sub-problems and finally prints the minimum cost starting from index 0. All the other code is just I/O helpers, encrypted string loaders, fake branches, and decompiler junk.

Description_Simple:
Title: Minimum Jump Cost Dynamic Programming Solver

Main goal: Compute the minimum total cost to travel from the first element to the last in an integer array, where you may jump forward by at most K positions and each jump’s cost is the absolute difference between start and landing values.

This code implements a top-down recursive DP with memoization (`minCostFrom`) in the `solve` method. It checks boundary conditions (beyond end = “infinite” cost, landing exactly on the last index = zero cost), then tries every jump length from 1 to K, accumulating the minimum cost of `abs(arr[i] – arr[i+step]) + solve(i+step)`. The `main` method reads N, K, and the array, initializes the memo array to –1, and prints `solve(0)`.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This is an obfuscated implementation of the classic 1-D “frog‐jump” DP problem. You have an array H of n heights and a maximum jump distance k. Starting at index 0, the frog may jump from i to any j in (i+1,…,i+k) (as long as j<n), paying cost |H[i]−H[j]| for each jump. The goal is to reach index n−1 with minimum total cost. The code uses a top-down recursive routine with a memo array `minCostFrom` (initialized to –1) to cache results; it returns 0 when at the last stone and ∞ (Integer.MAX_VALUE) if you run off the end. At each position it tries all legal jumps up to k ahead, picks the minimum cost of (|height diff| + cost from the landing stone), stores it in the memo, and returns it. The main method reads n, k and the heights, then outputs `solve(0)`.

Description_Simple:

Main Goal: The program reads three numbers N, P, and K, then reads N integer values v[i]. For each v[i], it computes an adjusted value P – 0.006 × v[i] and finds which one is closest to K. It then prints the 1-based index of the value whose adjusted result has the smallest absolute difference from K.

Details:

- solveB() implements the core logic:  
  1. Read N (number of items), P (base value), and K (target).  
  2. Loop i=0..N–1: read v[i], compute adj = P – 0.006*v[i], track |adj – K|.  
  3. Remember the index with the smallest difference.  
  4. Output that index + 1.  
- The code also contains stub methods for problems A, C, D, E, F (unused here) and string decryption routines for obfuscation, but only solveB() is actually invoked.
Description_Detailed:
This program’s real job is very simple:  
1. Read three integers from standard input:  
   • N = the number of measurements  
   • I₀ = a base value  
   • T = a target value  
2. Read N integer measurements x₁…xₙ.  
3. For each measurement xᵢ compute  
     yᵢ = I₀ – xᵢ × 0.006  
4. Find the index i whose yᵢ is closest (in absolute value) to T.  
5. Print that index (1-based).  

All of the other methods, encrypted literals, fake branches, etc., are just obfuscation around this core logic.

Description_Simple:

If no task meets the deadline (i.e. there is no valid cost ≤ T), it prints an obfuscated “TLE” (time limit exceeded) message.

2. BTimeLimitExceeded.solve:
   - Reads N (number of tasks) and T (time limit).
   - Initializes minCost = 10001.
   - Loops over the N task entries, each given as (cost, time).
   - If time ≤ T, updates minCost = min(minCost, cost).
   - After the loop:
     • If no valid task was found (minCost > 1000), prints “TLE” (decrypted at runtime via Blowfish).
     • Otherwise prints minCost.
3. Main: Sets up FastScanner and PrintWriter, then calls the solver.

Description_Simple:

Main Goal: The program reads an integer T (the number of test values) and then T integers. For each odd integer, it checks five specific compound divisibility conditions (divisible by 3, 13, 45; by 3, 13, 11; by 3, 13, 13; by 27, 13; and by 27, 45), increments a running total for each condition met, and finally prints the total count of all matches.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The program reads a single integer N from standard input and then, for every odd k from 1 to N, checks five “divisibility patterns,” incrementing a counter each time one of them holds:
 1. k divisible by 3, 5, and 7 (i.e. 105)
 2. k divisible by 3, 5, and 11 (165)
 3. k divisible by 3, 5, and 13 (195)
 4. k divisible by 5 and 27 (135)
 5. k divisible by 7 and 27 (189)

Because all the divisors are odd, the “odd-only” restriction doesn’t actually exclude any valid multiples. Thus the final result is just

    ⌊N/105⌋ + ⌊N/165⌋ + ⌊N/195⌋ + ⌊N/135⌋ + ⌊N/189⌋

which the program prints.

Title: Obfuscated String‐Comparison and Code‐Printer

Main Goal:
This program reads a line of user input, compares it against a set of secret strings that have been hidden by XOR, Blowfish, or DES encryption, and then prints various integer codes depending on which (if any) hidden string the input matches.

Summary of Key Functions:

1. lIlllllIIl():
   - Builds an array of integer constants (`IlIIIIll`) by using bitwise and length operations.

2. IIlllllIIl():
   - Creates the string array (`lIIIIIll`) of “secret” values by decoding literal Base64 tokens and then:
     a. XOR‐decoding via llIllllIIl()
     b. Blowfish‐decrypting via lIIllllIIl()
     c. DES‐decrypting via IlIllllIIl()

3. llIllllIIl(String, String):
   - Decodes the first argument from Base64, then XORs each character with the repeating key given in the second argument.

4. lIIllllIIl(String, String):
   - Uses MD5(key) → 128-bit Blowfish key to decrypt the first argument (after Base64 decode).

5. IlIllllIIl(String, String):
   - Uses MD5(key), truncated to 8 bytes → DES key to decrypt the first argument (after Base64 decode).

6. main(String[]):
   - Reads one line from standard input.
   - Performs a series of boolean checks comparing that input to the decoded secret strings.
   - According to which comparisons succeed or fail, prints out one of the integer constants from `IlIIIIll`.

In short, the code is a simple password/keyword checker, cleverly hidden behind multiple layers of decoding and obfuscation.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This is essentially a keyword‐matcher that reads one line of input, compares it against a fixed list of secret strings (which are stored encrypted in static arrays and decrypted at startup), and prints a small integer code depending on which secret was entered (or which combination of tests succeeds/fails). All of the obfuscation (bogus locals, fake branches, encrypted literals, renamed methods) is just noise – the real behavior is:

1. Decrypt a fixed list of ~18 secret strings when the class is loaded.
2. Read one input line from the user.
3. Check that input against several of those secrets in a few if-statements.
4. For each matching (or non-matching) case, print a corresponding integer (drawn from another small array of constants).

In other words, it’s not doing any complex algorithm or data processing – it’s just a simple “if the input equals X, print code A; if it equals Y, print code B; … otherwise print code Z” dispatch routine hiding its actual string constants behind run‐time decryption.

Description_Simple:
Title: Harshad Number Checker  
Main goal: Read an integer N, compute the sum of its decimal digits, and print “Yes” if N is divisible by that sum (i.e. N is a Harshad number), otherwise print “No”.  

The code is heavily obfuscated—it includes  
- a custom FastScanner for input,  
- runtime decryption routines (DES/MD5, Blowfish) to hide the “Yes”/“No” literals,  
- and an inner Solver class that parses N, accumulates its digit sum, tests `N % sum == 0`, and outputs the appropriate decrypted message.
Description_Detailed: This program reads a single integer N from standard input, computes the sum of its decimal digits, and then tests whether N is divisible by that digit‐sum.  If the remainder is zero, it prints “YES”; otherwise it prints “NO.”  All the convoluted branching, fake variables, encrypted string literals, and control‐flow junk are just obfuscation layers—the actual algorithm is the classic Harshad (Niven)‐number check.

Description_Simple:
Title: Finding the k-th number with exactly d “00” suffixes

Main goal:
Given two integers d and k, this program computes the k-th positive integer that is divisible by 100^d but not by 100^(d+1). In other words, it finds the k-th number whose decimal representation ends with exactly 2·d zeros (no more).

How it works:
1. It reads d and k from standard input.
2. It sets base = 100^d.
3. It maintains a running total x, initially 0.
4. It loops k times, each time:
   a. Increments x by base.
   b. Counts how many times 100 divides x (function howMany).
   c. If that count exceeds d (meaning x has >2·d trailing zeros), it adds base one more time to skip that “bad” number.
5. After k iterations, it prints x.
6. The helper howMany(n) repeatedly divides n by 100 and counts how many times it can do so (the exponent of 100 in n). The custom InputReader is just a fast I/O utility.

Thus the output is the k-th multiple of 100^d that is not divisible by 100^(d+1).
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The program reads two integers n and m. It sets B = 100^n and then loops m times, accumulating a total T which starts at 0 and gains B each iteration. Whenever the loop index i (1-based) is divisible by 57^(n+1), the code gives an extra B bonus for that iteration. In closed form it prints

    T = B * m  +  B * ⌊m / 57^(n+1)⌋

i.e. T = 100^n * ( m + ⌊m / 57^(n+1)⌋ ).

Description_Simple:
Title: Total Power-of-Two Divisibility Counter

Main goal: The program reads an integer n and then n more integers, and for each input number it checks divisibility by 2, 4, 8, 16, … up to 2^29. It counts one point for every power-of-two divisor each number has, effectively summing the exponent of 2 in the prime factorization (the number of trailing zero bits) across all inputs, then prints that total.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The program reads an integer N, then reads N integer values into an array. It then, for each array element, repeatedly tests divisibility by successive powers of two (2, 4, 8, 16, … up to 2^29). Every time an element is evenly divisible by the current power-of-two, it increments a running total. Because an integer divisible by 2^k is also divisible by all lower powers of two, the net effect is that for each element it counts how many times 2 divides it (i.e. the exponent of 2 in its prime factorization, or “number of trailing zero bits”) and adds that to the total. Finally it prints the sum of these counts across all N inputs.

Description_Simple:
Title: Find Largest Perfect Power ≤ N

Main Goal:
Given an integer N, the code finds the greatest integer M (1 < M ≤ N) whose prime‐factorization exponents are all equal and greater than 1 (i.e. M = X^k for some integer X and k > 1, examples: 4, 8, 9, 16, 27, 36, …). If no such M exists, it prints 1.

How it works in brief:
1. Build a smallest‐prime‐factor (SPF) sieve for all integers up to 1000.
2. Read the input N.
3. Iterate M = N down to 2:
   a. Factorize M using the SPF array, count the exponent of each prime.
   b. Check if all recorded exponents are identical and exceed 1.
   c. If yes, print M and terminate.
4. If the loop ends without finding any, print 1.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program first builds an integer array `spf[1..1000]` by a simple sieve‐like loop so that for each `n>1`, `spf[n]` becomes its largest prime divisor.  Then it reads a single integer N and searches downward from N to find the biggest M≤N whose prime‐factorization exponents are all ≥2—in other words, M is a nontrivial perfect power (xᵏ with k≥2).  As soon as it finds such an M, it prints M and exits.  If it never finds one (i.e. N<4), it falls through and prints 1.

Description_Simple:
Title: Bitter Alchemy Solver

Main Goal:  
This code reads an integer n (number of elements), an integer m (target sum), and an array of n positive integers. It then computes and outputs  
  n + ⌊(m – sum_of_array) / min_element⌋  
that is, starting from n items with total size sum_of_array, how many additional items of minimum size can fit into the remaining capacity (m – sum_of_array).

Description of Key Components:  
1. Class Main  
   - Contains the entry point, sets up input (FastScanner) and output (PrintWriter), and invokes BBitterAlchemy.solve with a hard-coded parameter (1).  

2. FastScanner  
   - A custom, buffered scanner to read ints, longs, and arrays from System.in quickly.  

3. BBitterAlchemy  
   - solve(int dummy, FastScanner in, PrintWriter out):  
       • Reads n and m.  
       • Reads an array of n integers, sorts it, computes its sum and minimum.  
       • Calculates result = n + (m – sum) / minimum_element.  
       • Prints result.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads two integers N and M, then an array A of N integers. It sorts A in ascending order and computes the sum S of all elements. Let a₁ = the smallest element of A. It then calculates and outputs

    answer = N + ⌊(M – S) / a₁⌋

In other words, starting from the initial N items with total cost S, it uses any remaining budget (M – S) to “buy” additional items at the cheapest available cost a₁, and reports the total number of items possible.

Description_Simple:
Title: Minimizing Purchase Cost with Combo Deals  
Main goal: Calculate the lowest total cost to buy a specified number of two products (d of type A and e of type B), given individual prices a and b and a special “combo” price c (which covers one of each when buying two).  
Briefly, the code:
1. Reads five integers a, b, c, d, e.  
2. Computes how many pairs of A+B to buy (the smaller of d and e) using the cheaper of (a+b) vs. (2·c).  
3. For the remaining |d–e| items, chooses the cheaper of the individual price (a or b) vs. (2·c) per item.  
4. Sums these costs and prints the minimal total.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The de‐obfuscated program reads five integers a, b, c, d, e from standard input and computes a single integer result as follows:

1. Let x=d, y=e  
2. Compute  
   • lo = min(x, y)  
   • hi = max(x, y)  
   • diff = |x − y|  
3. Decide a “base” value:  
   if (a + b) ≥ c then  
     base = lo * c  
   else  
     base = lo * (a + b)  
4. Decide a “multiplier” f:  
   if hi came from d (i.e. d ≥ e) then  
     f = min(a, c)  
   else  
     f = min(b, c)  
5. The final result = base + diff * f  

Finally, it prints that result. The various obfuscated branches and dead‐code all boil down to this simple min/max‐and‐multiply logic.

Description_Simple:
Title: Counting Elements on Either Side of a Pivot

Main goal:
Given three inputs N, M and K and then M distinct integers (each between 1 and N–1 and not equal to K), the code counts how many of the M numbers lie to the “left” of K (i.e. < K) and how many lie to the “right” of K (i.e. > K), then prints the smaller of those two counts.

Brief explanation:
1. Read N (1 ≤ N ≤ 100), M (1 ≤ M ≤ 100), and K (1 ≤ K ≤ N–1).
2. Read an array of M values, each in [1, N–1] and not equal to K.
3. Count how many values are greater than K.
4. Count how many values are less than K.
5. Output the minimum of these two counts.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads three integers a, b, c (with 1 ≤ a,b ≤ 100 and 1 ≤ c < a), then reads b further integers (each between 1 and a–1) into an array. It then computes two totals:

1. S₁ = ∑_{x=c to a–1} (number of array elements ≥ x)  
2. S₂ = ∑_{x=0 to c}   (number of array elements ≥ x)  

Finally it prints the smaller of S₁ and S₂.

In other words, for each threshold x in the two ranges [c, a–1] and [0, c], it counts how many of the b values meet or exceed x, sums those counts in each range, and outputs the minimum of those two sums.

Description_Simple:
Title: Simple Integer Multiplication  
Main Goal: Reads two integers from standard input and outputs their product.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads two integers from standard input and outputs their product. It uses a fast input scanner to read the first integer (n) and the second integer, multiplies them (n × second), prints the result to standard output, and flushes the output.

Description_Simple:

Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads an integer N, then reads N more integers into an array. It sorts that array in descending order, then splits the sorted list into two running totals by alternating indices: values at even indices (0, 2, 4, …) go into sum A, and values at odd indices (1, 3, 5, …) go into sum B. Finally, it prints the difference A – B. All of the obfuscation (weird names, bogus branches, encrypted strings, dead code, etc.) hides this simple “sort and take turns summing” logic, and the auxiliary class is just a hand-rolled fast I/O routine.

Description_Simple:

Description_Simple:
Title: Counting Combinations for a Target Sum using 2000, 100, and 50‐Value Units

Main goal:
This program reads four integers A, B, C, and X. It treats A, B, and C as the maximum allowed counts of items worth 2000, 100, and 50 units respectively, and X as a target sum. It then counts and prints the number of nonnegative integer solutions (i, j, k) with 0 ≤ i ≤ A, 0 ≤ j ≤ B, 0 ≤ k ≤ C such that

  2000·i + 100·j + 50·k = X.

Functions and structure:
- A static array holds the three denominations: 2000, 100, 50.
- Helper boolean methods test (a) equality, (b) nonzero, (c) zero, and (d) ≥ 0 to drive the control flow.
- Depending on which of A, B, C are nonzero, the code uses one, two, or three nested loops to enumerate all valid combinations within the given limits.
- Each time the sum equals X, a counter is incremented.
- Finally, the program prints the total count of valid combinations.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads four integers from standard input: three “limits” (let’s call them X, Y, Z) and a target value T. It then has three hidden coefficients (let’s call them A, B, C) initialized once at class load time. The core logic simply counts how many non‐negative integer triples (i, j, k), with i < X, j < Y, k < Z, satisfy the linear equation

    A·i + B·j + C·k == T

It special‐cases any zero limit (X, Y or Z equal to zero) by dropping that dimension from the loops (so it effectively handles the 1D, 2D or 3D counting problem uniformly). Finally, it prints the total count of solutions. The convoluted gotos, fake branches, encrypted strings and meaningless variables are all just obfuscation layered on top of this simple counting routine.

Description_Simple:
Title: Maximum Profit from a Single Buy‐Sell Transaction

Main goal:
This program reads an integer n from standard input, then reads n more integers into an array. It scans the array to find the largest difference arr[j] – arr[i] with j > i (the maximum “profit” you could get by buying once at a low value and selling once later at a high value). Finally it prints that maximal difference.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads an integer n from stdin, then reads n more integers into an array. It treats the array as a sequence of “prices” and computes the maximum difference arr[j] − arr[i] with j>i (i.e. the largest gain you could get by “buying” at an earlier index and “selling” later). It initializes the best difference to arr[1]−arr[0], scans through the list, keeps track of the smallest value seen so far, and updates the best difference whenever a larger arr[k]−minSeen is found. Finally it prints that maximum difference (which may be negative if the sequence is strictly decreasing).

Description_Simple:
Title: Parity Checker for Two Integers

Main Goal:
This Java program reads two integers from standard input and prints "Odd" if both numbers are odd, otherwise it prints "Even".

Key Components:
1. Static Initialization:
   - Defines an integer array `llIllIllIl` = {2, 1, 0}.
   - Defines a string array (via obfuscated decryption) with messages: index 0 = "Odd", index 1 = "Even".

2. Decryption Function (`IIllIIlIIlIl`):
   - Decodes a Base64‐encoded string and XORs each byte with a key to obtain the human‐readable labels ("Odd"/"Even").

3. Fast Scanner Class (`FS`):
   - Provides methods to efficiently read tokens, ints, and longs from `System.in`.

4. `main` Method:
   - Uses `FS.nextInt()` twice to read two integers.
   - Checks `(first % 2 == 1) && (second % 2 == 1)`.
   - If true, prints the decrypted string at index 0 ("Odd"); otherwise prints index 1 ("Even").
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads two integers from standard input, tests whether each one is odd (i.e. `value % 2 == 1`), and then prints one of two fixed messages depending on the result. If both inputs are odd, it prints the first decrypted string; otherwise it prints the second decrypted string. All of the convoluted renaming, dummy branches, control‐flow gymnastics, and on‐the‐fly Base64/XOR string decryption are just obfuscation layers around this simple “both-odd?” check and conditional print.

Description_Simple:
Title: Perfect Square Checker

Main goal: This obfuscated Java program reads two tokens from standard input, concatenates them to form an integer, and determines whether that integer is a perfect square. It prints a decrypted “YES” message if the number is a perfect square, or a decrypted “NO” message otherwise.

Key components:
- main: reads input, computes integer and its integer square‐root, compares square.
- IlIllIIIll: decrypts Base64‐encoded strings (“YES”/“NO”) using DES with an MD5‐derived key.
- IIIlIlIIll & lllIIlIIll: initialize integer and string arrays for obfuscation.
- FastScanner: efficient input reader for tokens, integers, longs, doubles.
Description_Detailed: The obfuscated program simply reads two space‐separated strings, concatenates them (e.g. “12” + “34” → “1234”), parses the result as an integer N, computes ⌊√N⌋, squares it and checks whether it equals N (i.e. tests if N is a perfect square). It then prints one of two hard‐coded (but encrypted/decoded at class‐load time) messages—“Yes” if N is a perfect square, “No” otherwise. The bulk of the noise is just control‐flow junk, renamed identifiers, dead‐code and string‐encryption routines.

Description_Simple:
Title: Manhattan Travel Validator

Main Goal: Determine if a traveler can visit a given sequence of points (x, y) at specified times t, moving at most one Manhattan‐unit per time unit and respecting parity (even/odd) constraints. The program reads N triplets (t, x, y), checks for each leg (from (0,0) to the first point and then point to point) that
  •  |Δx|+|Δy| ≤ Δt 
  •  (|Δx|+|Δy|) mod 2 == Δt mod 2
If any check fails it immediately prints “No” (two different error cases both decode to “No” via XOR and DES), otherwise at the end it prints “Yes” (decoded via Blowfish).

Key Components:
  •  Obfuscated integer constants in array l[] to represent 0,1,2,3,4.
  •  Three decryption routines:
     –  XOR + Base64 for I[0]
     –  DES + MD5 for I[2]
     –  Blowfish + MD5 for I[1]
     These yield the strings “No” (twice) and “Yes”.  
  •  Main logic in main(): read input, perform the distance/time and parity checks, print result, exit.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads an integer N and then N triples of integers (A[i], B[i], C[i]). It walks through these triples in order, and for each index i it computes:

 • If i == 0 (the first triple):  
   p = |B[0]|, q = |C[0]|, a = A[0].

 • If i > 0 (any subsequent triple):  
   p = |B[i] − B[i−1]|, q = |C[i] − C[i−1]|, a = A[i] − A[i−1]|.

It then checks two conditions simultaneously:
  1. The “sum” condition: (p + q) must not exceed a.  
  2. The “parity” condition: (p + q) and a must have opposite parity (one even, one odd).

If both are violated (i.e. p + q > a **and** (p + q) % 2 == a % 2), the program immediately prints an error message and exits. The error message depends on whether the failure happened at i = 0 or at i > 0 (two different predefined strings). If the loop completes without triggering an exit, the program prints a third “success” message.

In short, it’s a validator: it reads a sequence of cost/coordinate‐change triples, enforces a “triangle‐inequality plus parity‐mismatch” rule between each point (or from the origin for the first), and reports failure at the first violation or reports success if all checks pass.

Description_Simple:

Main goal: Read an integer N, then read N more integers and output the count of distinct values among them.

Brief overview:

- Main: sets up IO, calls BKagamiMochi.solve().
- BKagamiMochi.solve(): reads N, loops N times adding each integer to a HashSet, then prints the HashSet’s size.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
This program reads an integer N from standard input, then reads N more integers and counts how many distinct values appear. Internally it uses a FastScanner for buffered reading and a HashSet<Integer> to track unique numbers; finally it prints the size of that set.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Java Solver for the “Otoshidama”‐Style Bill‐Counting Problem

Main Goal:
  Read two integers N (the total number of bills) and Y (the total amount of money), and find nonnegative counts (a, b, c) of three bill types that
    1. a + b + c = N  
    2. 10000·a + 5000·b + 1000·c = Y  
  If such a solution exists, print “a b c”; otherwise print “-1 -1 -1”.

How It Works:
  • The code is heavily obfuscated—integers and string literals are hidden behind bit‐shifts, XORs, Blowfish/MD5 decryption, and odd loop‐conditions.  
  • In main(), it reads N and Y via a custom FastScanner, then tries all 0 ≤ a, b ≤ N, computes c = N - a - b, and checks the two equations.  
  • When it finds a valid triple, it prints them separated by spaces (the separators are decrypted at startup).  
  • If no triple is found after exhausting the loops, it prints the fallback string “-1 -1 -1” (also decrypted).  
  • Utility methods (llIIIlllll, llIllIllll, lllIlIllll, lIIllIllll) initialize constants and decrypt the few hard-coded strings; the FastScanner class handles fast I/O.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>  
The program reads two integers N and Y. It looks for non‐negative counts i, j, k (representing numbers of 10 000 yen, 5 000 yen, and 1 000 yen bills) that satisfy  
  1. i + j + k = N  
  2. 10 000·i + 5 000·j + 1 000·k = Y  

If such a triple exists, it prints “i j k” (space‐separated). If no solution is found, it prints “-1 -1 -1.” Internally it divides Y by 1 000 to simplify the arithmetic and then does a double loop over i and j (0…N), computes k = N – i – j, checks the two constraints, and stops when a valid combination is found.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Sum of Numbers by Factorial‐Base Digit‐Sum

Main goal: Read three integers N, L, R; then compute and print the sum of all i from 1 to N whose sum of “factorial‐base” digits lies between L and R inclusive.  

Description:
- The code is heavily obfuscated (CFR‐decompiled, weird naming, boolean wrappers, and bit-trick constants) but boils down to:
  1. FastScanner reads three ints: N (= upper limit), L (= lower bound on digit sum), R (= upper bound on digit sum).
  2. A loop from i=1 to N computes the sum of the coefficients in i’s factorial number system (factoradic) representation.
     - For i<2: digit‐sum = i
     - For 2≤i<3: digit‐sum = (i mod 2) + (i/2)
     - For 3≤i<4: digit‐sum = (i mod 2) + (i mod 3)/2 + (i/3)
     - For 4≤i<5 and similarly for higher i up to base 5, then a catch‐all for i≥5.
  3. If L ≤ (factorial‐base digit‐sum) ≤ R, then add i to the running total.
  4. Print the final total.
- Unused utility methods for gcd, lcm, and primality testing are present but not invoked in main.
Description_Detailed:
<summary_description>
The program reads three integers n, a, b and then computes the sum of all i in 1…n whose binary‐digit sum (popcount) lies between a and b inclusive. It does this by “unrolling” small ranges (i<2, i<4, i<8, i<16) with explicit bit‐sum formulas, and a catch‐all for larger i, but all the convoluted branches boil down to checking a ≤ popcount(i) ≤ b and adding i to the running total. Finally it prints the resulting sum. The rest of the code (gcd, lcm, isPrime, encrypted strings, weird gotos, fake locals, etc.) is purely obfuscation and never factors into this core logic.

Description_Simple:
Title: Counting Occurrences of a Secret Token Using Decrypted Delimiter

Main Goal:
This code decrypts two hard-coded Base64 strings (one with DES, one with Blowfish using MD5-derived keys) to recover:
 1) A delimiter string  
 2) A target token string  
It then reads a line of input, splits it on the decrypted delimiter, counts how many of the resulting substrings exactly match the decrypted token, and prints that count.

Key Components:
- Static initialization decrypts and populates `lIllIllIl[0]` (the delimiter) and `lIllIllIl[1]` (the token to count).
- `hayami` is a custom fast-scanner implementation that provides `nextHayami()` to read the next whitespace-delimited token from `System.in`.
- `main()` calls `nextHayami()` once to get the full input line, splits it by the decrypted delimiter, iterates through the parts, increments a counter whenever a part equals the decrypted token, and finally prints the counter.
Description_Detailed:
This program reads a single line (token) from standard input, decrypts two hidden string literals at class‐load time to recover (1) a delimiter and (2) a “skip” marker, then splits the input line on that delimiter. It iterates over the resulting array of substrings, counts how many of them are *not* equal to the marker, and prints that count.  

Underneath the obfuscation, there are just:
 • A small I/O helper (`hayami`) that behaves like a `Scanner` (it skips whitespace, reads tokens, ints, longs, doubles, etc.).  
 • In `Main`, on `main()` it calls `nextHayami()` once to get the entire input string, splits it by the decrypted delimiter, loops through each piece, increments a counter for every piece not matching the decrypted marker, and finally outputs the counter.

Description_Simple:
Title: “Obfuscated Fast I/O and Count‐Divisions‐By‐Two”
Main Goal: Read an integer N and an array of N integers, then repeatedly divide all array elements by 2 until at least one element becomes odd, finally outputting how many full division‐rounds were completed.

This code is split into two parts:

1. Class hayami:
   • Acts as a highly obfuscated fast scanner.  
   • Wraps System.in in a byte buffer and provides methods to read the next token as String, int, long or double (nextHayami, saori_hayami, saorihayami, Hayamin).  
   • Handles whitespace skipping, numeric parsing, sign handling and throws NoSuchElementException or NumberFormatException on invalid input.

2. Class Main:
   • Uses hayami to read:
       – N = saori_hayami()  
       – An array A of N integers via repeated saori_hayami().
   • Then enters a loop:

Description_Simple:

Because n itself is always one of its “factor” pair members and has the most digits, the result is just the digit‐count of n.

Description_Simple:

Description_Simple: This Java program defines and decrypts a large table of string constants at startup, then reads three whitespace‐separated inputs from the user. All of the obfuscated loops, bogus branches, XOR/Blowfish/DES string‐decryptors, and renamed variables are just window‐dressing: at its heart it’s a simple three‐state automaton that routes one of three inputs to one of three printed outcomes.
